# .dotfiles: A shell environment in scripts

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/dotfiles/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/dotfiles/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/.dotfiles
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 52ff3c19bdebfbebf1d9e320fff199044bdf5e13

## Summary

These dotfiles collect the shell and editor setup I used across machines. The installer manages packages, configuration files and upstream projects.

**Why it exists:** Idempotent multi-distribution installer supporting apt, dnf, pacman with modular Zsh and Vim configurations.

**Best fit:** Reproducible shell and developer environment across macOS and Linux servers.

## Use cases

Bash scripts that install, update and remove a Linux shell setup: vimrc, Oh My Zsh, tmux and dev tools.

- **Install the vimrc setup** (Developer, Upstream projects): install_vimrc in install.sh installs vim and git, clones amix/vimrc into ~/.vim_runtime and runs its installer; edit_vimrc moves NERDTree to the left and turns on line numbers.
- **Set up Oh My Zsh and tmux** (Developer, Upstream projects): install_oh_my_zsh downloads the official Oh My Zsh installer with wget; edit_oh_my_zsh switches the theme and writes a minimal prompt theme; install_tmux writes a full ~/.tmux.conf.
- **Install dev toolchains** (Developer, OS package manager): bash install.sh &lt;option&gt; runs one installer (Python, JDK, nvm, .NET, Go, Rust, Docker, kubectl, AWS CLI, Azure CLI, JupyterLab, network tools); install_package reads /etc/os-release to pick apt-get, pacman, dnf, yum or brew.
- **Update the scripts and vimrc** (Developer, Upstream projects): update.sh defines update_install_script (git pull, then bash install.sh) and update_vimrc (git pull --rebase in ~/.vim_runtime, then update_plugins.py); the file only defines them, so it is meant to be sourced.
- **Remove tools with backups** (Developer, OS package manager): uninstall.sh copies ~/.vimrc and ~/.tmux.conf to .backup files before deleting them, and purges JDK, Python, Rust, Go, Jupyter, AWS CLI, Azure CLI and nvm; run with bash, it calls every uninstall function in turn.
- **Show neofetch at login** (Developer, OS package manager): motd/motd.sh installs neofetch with apt-get when missing and writes /etc/update-motd.d/10-neofetch so the system summary appears in the login banner.

### Scenario: Set up a fresh Ubuntu machine

1. Clone the repository and run bash install.sh with no option to print the usage() list.
2. Run bash install.sh install_vimrc to install vim and git and clone amix/vimrc into ~/.vim_runtime.
3. Run bash install.sh install_oh_my_zsh, then install_tmux, to get zsh and a written ~/.tmux.conf.
4. Run bash install.sh install_docker; it fetches get.docker.com and Docker Compose 1.29.2.
5. On a server, run motd/motd.sh as root so neofetch shows at each SSH login.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Shell | 100 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Installation

```bash
bash install.sh
source install.sh
install_vimrc
```


## Features and components

- **Package installation** — install.sh reads the distribution from /etc/os-release, then selects apt, pacman, dnf or yum. exec_root wraps commands that need elevated privileges. Package installation and configuration changes therefore share one script.
- **Editor and shell setup** — The Vim path installs amix/vimrc and applies local changes, including line numbers and the file-tree position. Other functions install Oh My Zsh. update.sh and uninstall.sh are separate maintenance entry points.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- install.sh → Distribution detection
- Distribution detection → System packages
- System packages → Vim and Zsh configuration

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;install.sh&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Distribution detection&#34;]
  n2[&#34;System packages&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Vim and Zsh configuration&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
```

**One path through the code:** Follow install_vimrc from its package request to the upstream clone, then to the edits in ~/.vim_runtime. This shows which files the installer owns and which belong to another project.

## Constraints and checks

The script edits home-directory files and runs privileged package commands. Back up existing configuration and inspect each function before running it on a current machine.

## Files to read

- [install.sh](https://github.com/antoinebou12/.dotfiles/blob/main/install.sh)
- [update.sh](https://github.com/antoinebou12/.dotfiles/blob/main/update.sh)
- [uninstall.sh](https://github.com/antoinebou12/.dotfiles/blob/main/uninstall.sh)

# AINewsTracker: Financial news analysis and backtesting

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/ainewstracker/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/ainewstracker/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/AlgoETS/AINewsTracker
- Inspected revision: 74a8366f5c19e352277a74381559e310e9cf959c


## Use cases

FastAPI service from AlgoÉTS that collects financial news, scores it with FinBERT and stores it in MongoDB.

- **Fetch news from a source** (Quant analyst, News feeds and APIs): The /news routes pull the Financial Modeling Prep 8-K RSS feed, GNews or a named feed with feedparser, download each article&#39;s text and save it; limits above 10 run as background tasks.
- **Score article sentiment** (Quant analyst): TextMetrics loads ProsusAI/finbert for sentiment, Jean-Baptiste/roberta-ticker for ticker extraction and distilbart-cnn-12-6 for summaries; GET /articles/{article_id}/score returns the stored score.
- **Query news by company** (Quant analyst): /company stores tickers, and /articles/articles_by_company_id/{company_id} or POST /articles/articles_by_company_ids return the articles linked to one or more companies.
- **Seed companies and news** (Quant analyst, News feeds and APIs): POST /seed/seed_companies and /seed/seed_news start CompanySeeder and NewsSeeder in the background; NewsSeeder reads Financial Modeling Prep stock news with FMP_API_KEY and saves the articles to MongoDB.
- **Serve scored articles** (Backtesting service): GET /v1/articles, protected by a Bearer service token (AINEWSTRACKER_SERVICE_TOKEN), returns articles filtered by symbols and time window with sentiment label, probabilities and model name, paged by cursor.

### Scenario: Collect and query Apple news locally

1. Copy .env.example to .env, set FMP_API_KEY, then run docker-compose up --build to start the API with MongoDB and Redis.
2. Open http://localhost:8000/api/v1/docs and call POST /seed/seed_companies.
3. Call POST /seed/seed_news; NewsSeeder reads Financial Modeling Prep stock news in the background and stores the scored articles.
4. Read the stored articles with GET /articles/ and check one with GET /articles/{article_id}/score.
5. From a backtesting service, call GET /v1/articles?symbols=AAPL with the Bearer service token.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 88.92 |
| Shell | 8.19 |
| Dockerfile | 2.9 |

# another-install-script: A menu for homelab installation

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/another-install-script/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/another-install-script/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/another-install-script
- License: GPL-3.0
- Inspected revision: 6e1e193260504106593f6b92bb799aacafdf0e2b

## Summary

another-install-script is a shell entry point for choosing system setup and container installations. Its structure separates the menu from the service definitions so that adding a service does not require putting every command in setup.sh.

**Why it exists:** Interactive TUI shell installer automating deployment of Docker containers and server configurations.

**Best fit:** One-command server provisioning for homelabs and development VPS.

## Use cases

Whiptail menu in Bash that installs base tools and Docker Compose services on a personal Ubuntu server.

- **Install base server tools** (Server admin): The Installation entry of main_setup_menu (src/menu.sh) shows a checklist: basic packages, Docker, Cockpit, LXDE, Ansible, Dokku, Vagrant and more; src/install.sh runs the selected items.
- **Deploy selected containers** (Server admin, Docker Engine): Add Container lists the folders under containers/; each &lt;name&gt;.sh runs docker-compose up -d on the docker-compose.yml next to it (for example containers/gogs/).
- **Open ports for containers** (Server admin, UFW firewall): After containers are added, manage_firewall_ports_allow_list in src/firewall.sh reads their ports from config.yml and allows them; with system.firewall set to yes, ufw denies other incoming traffic but keeps SSH, 2222, HTTP and HTTPS.
- **Remove installed containers** (Server admin, Docker Engine): remove_container_menu shows the installed containers; each remove_docker_&lt;name&gt; function runs docker-compose down on that service.
- **Uninstall the setup** (Server admin, Docker Engine, UFW firewall): The Uninstall entry runs uninstall.sh, which loads the src/ modules to undo the setup. The Backup entry currently calls the same script; the backup helpers in src/backup.sh are not wired to the menu.

### Scenario: Provision a new VPS with a few self-hosted services

1. Clone the repository and run sudo bash setup.sh; it opens main_setup_menu because bashmenu is yes in config.yml.
2. Choose Installation and keep basic and docker checked; selecting docker opens the container list next.
3. Tick services such as gogs and bookstack; each script runs docker-compose up -d.
4. Let the firewall step allow the ports listed in config.yml and enable ufw.
5. Later, use Remove Container to stop a service with docker-compose down.

| --- | ---: |


```bash
git pull --recurse-submodules
git submodule update --remote
cd docs/generator
chmod &#43;x generate_docs.sh
bash generate_docs.sh ../docs.md
```


## Features and components

- **Entry point and menus** — setup.sh sources src/menu.sh and calls main_setup_menu. The root script handles arguments, while the sourced module controls navigation. config.yml sits beside the launcher as the project’s configuration surface.
- **Service definitions** — The containers directory holds installation material for individual services. Keeping that material outside the menu makes the repository easier to extend, but each installation still changes the host or its Docker environment.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- setup.sh → src/menu.sh
- src/menu.sh → Configuration and selection
- Configuration and selection → Container installation

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;setup.sh&#34;]
  n1[&#34;src/menu.sh&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Configuration and selection&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Container installation&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
```

**One path through the code:** Start with the main_setup_menu call, then inspect the selected service under containers before executing it. The menu is a dispatcher; the selected service determines the actual side effects.

## Constraints and checks

The README calls this a work in progress and records testing on an older Ubuntu release. Those notes do not establish compatibility with a current server.

# antoinebou12: How the GitHub profile is assembled

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/antoinebou12/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/antoinebou12/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/antoinebou12
- License: GPL-3.0
- Inspected revision: c519c6b47b35d3d391167aa43b6cf6cafe7d0435

## Summary

This is the repository behind my GitHub profile README. It combines ordinary Markdown with images, embedded widgets and scheduled updates. There is no application server in the profile itself.

**Why it exists:** Automated SVG and metrics rendering workflow maintaining dynamic profile assets.

**Best fit:** Automated profile asset generation.

## Use cases

GitHub profile README with links, badges, pinned projects and stats, kept current by scheduled Actions.

- **Read the profile and links** (Profile visitor): README.md opens with the platform and graphics headline, then links (GitHub, LinkedIn, website, CV, email), certification badges and the main languages and tools.
- **Browse pinned projects** (Profile visitor): A collapsible Featured projects section shows pin cards for repositories such as AINewsTracker, hass_renpho, ipc-toolkit and TrueMapData, plus the DashCTRL, ETSim and UFOKEK organisations.
- **Refresh 3D contribution chart** (GitHub Actions): github-profile-3d-contrib.yml runs daily at 05:00 UTC, generates the 3D contribution calendar, keeps only profile-night-green.svg and commits it.
- **Update LeetCode badges** (GitHub Actions): update-readme.yml runs daily at 12:00 UTC, fetches stats from leetcodestats.cyclic.app and rewrites the badges between the LEETCODE_STATS markers in README.md.
- **Check README links** (Profile owner, GitHub Actions): On each push or pull request to main or master, check-links.yml runs lychee on README.md and docs/**/*.md and writes a job summary.
- **Publish the Jekyll page** (Profile owner, GitHub Actions): jekyll-pages.yml builds docs/ with the jekyll-theme-primer theme and deploys it to GitHub Pages; docs/index.md points back to the profile README.

### Scenario: Edit the profile and let automation keep it current

1. The owner edits README.md, for example the Featured projects list, and pushes to master.
2. check-links.yml runs lychee on README.md and the docs Markdown and reports broken links.
3. jekyll-pages.yml builds docs/ and deploys the small Jekyll site to GitHub Pages.
4. Each day, github-profile-3d-contrib.yml regenerates profile-night-green.svg and commits it.
5. A visitor opens the profile page and sees the updated README, stats cards and 3D calendar.

## Features and components

- **README and assets** — README.md is the visible profile document. The images, models and profile-3d-contrib directories hold assets used alongside it. GitHub renders the document, while linked services may generate their own images separately.
- **Scheduled changes** — The update-readme workflow fetches LeetCode statistics, builds badge URLs and replaces the text between dedicated README markers. Separate workflows handle the contribution graphic, link checks and Pages.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- External statistics → GitHub Actions
- GitHub Actions → Marked README section
- Marked README section → GitHub profile

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;External statistics&#34;]
  n1[&#34;GitHub Actions&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Marked README section&#34;]
  n3[&#34;GitHub profile&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
```

**One path through the code:** In update-readme.yml, follow the HTTP response into the badge strings and then into the marker replacement. If either marker is missing, that replacement block is skipped.

## Constraints and checks

External badge endpoints can fail or become stale. A profile graphic is a presentation of a source’s data, not an independently verified measure of contribution quality.

## Files to read

- [README.md](https://github.com/antoinebou12/antoinebou12/blob/master/README.md)
- [.github/workflows/update-readme.yml](https://github.com/antoinebou12/antoinebou12/blob/master/.github/workflows/update-readme.yml)
- [.github/workflows/github-profile-3d-contrib.yml](https://github.com/antoinebou12/antoinebou12/blob/master/.github/workflows/github-profile-3d-contrib.yml)

# architecture: Architecture as editable documentation

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/architecture/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/architecture/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/architecture
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: a511b1a730ced19f6340548d5a46e20ae6e2df9b

## Summary

This archived repository stores a home-infrastructure diagram in several formats. Its architecture is a documentation workflow: editable sources produce diagrams that can be opened or viewed without a running application.

**Why it exists:** Editable home-infrastructure diagrams preserved as PlantUML and draw.io sources, with HTML and image exports.

**Best fit:** Reading an archived infrastructure snapshot or editing its diagram sources to document a homelab.

## Use cases

C4 PlantUML and draw.io diagrams of a home lab: Cloudflare, an OVH VPS, hypervisors, a NAS and services.

- **View the v1 draw.io diagram** (Reader, Diagram renderers): architecture.drawio.html embeds the draw.io XML in the diagrams.net viewer script, with zoom, layers and lightbox; the README links it as v1.
- **Render the v2 C4 diagram** (Reader, Diagram renderers): architecture.plantuml includes C4_Deployment, Font Awesome, OSA and Office icon sets; the README v2 link is an encoded render on the PlantUML server.
- **Trace external access paths** (Reader): The Rel lines show users reaching Cloudflare over HTTPS, Cloudflare forwarding to the OVH VPS, the VPS reaching the home and personal networks over WireGuard, and the admin using Teleport over SSH.
- **Inventory VMs and containers** (Reader): Deployment nodes list XCP-ng, Proxmox and Windows hosts, a QNAP NAS with a media stack, and VMs such as Talos (Portainer, AI News Tracker, Freqtrade), Home Assistant and Caddy with Prometheus and Grafana, each with CPU, RAM and disk properties.
- **Edit and re-export the diagram** (Diagram maintainer, Diagram renderers): The maintainer edits architecture.plantuml or architecture.drawio and exports a picture such as home architecture.png.

### Scenario: Follow a web request into the home lab

1. Open architecture.plantuml, or the v2 link in README.md rendered by the PlantUML server.
2. Start at the User person, who reaches Cloudflare (CDN and reverse proxy) over HTTPS.
3. Follow Cloudflare to the OVH VPS, which runs Caddy, Teleport and Uptime Kuma.
4. Follow the WireGuard link from the VPS to the Personal Network and its Proxmox host.
5. See the Caddy VM route traffic to AI News Tracker, Marketwatch, Portainer, Plex and Jellyfin.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| HTML | 100 |

## Features and components

- **Editable sources** — The root includes both a PlantUML source and a draw.io document. These are separate diagram representations. Their presence does not mean that one is automatically generated from the other.
- **Published views** — PNG and HTML files provide convenient viewing formats. The README links readers to those representations. The repository describes infrastructure; it does not deploy or monitor the services shown.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- PlantUML source → PlantUML rendering
- PlantUML rendering → Diagram image
- draw.io source → HTML and PNG export

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;PlantUML source&#34;]
  n1[&#34;PlantUML rendering&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Diagram image&#34;]
  n3[&#34;draw.io source&#34;]
  n4[&#34;HTML and PNG export&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Choose the editable format first, then compare its rendered view with the exported image. Keeping both paths visible helps prevent a screenshot from becoming the only surviving description of the system.

## Constraints and checks

This is an archived infrastructure snapshot. Service names and connections in a diagram do not prove that those services are still running or reachable.

## Files to read

- [README.md](https://github.com/antoinebou12/architecture/blob/main/README.md)
- [architecture.plantuml](https://github.com/antoinebou12/architecture/blob/main/architecture.plantuml)
- [architecture.drawio](https://github.com/antoinebou12/architecture/blob/main/architecture.drawio)

# Artemis-N3DS: Streaming within a dual-screen client

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/artemis-n3ds/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/artemis-n3ds/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/Artemis-N3DS
- License: GPL-3.0
- Inspected revision: c5eb0205ba4eb00f4fff96097d987b3267a7be08

## Summary

Artemis-N3DS adapts Moonlight Embedded to the Nintendo 3DS family. It combines host discovery and pairing with a console-specific interface, input handling and video presentation. The New 3DS hardware path is a particular concern.

**Why it exists:** Constrained systems engineering streaming 60fps video over 802.11n Wi-Fi to a dual-screen ARM11 device.

**Best fit:** Remote desktop and gaming on legacy Nintendo New 3DS hardware.

## Use cases

Moonlight Embedded fork that streams games from a Sunshine PC to a New 3DS, with a bottom-screen helper UI.

- **Install the CIA or 3DSX** (3DS player): dist/INSTALL.md describes installing artemis.cia from the HOME Menu with FBI, or copying artemis.3dsx to sd:/3ds/artemis/ for the Homebrew Launcher; custom firmware is required.
- **Pair with a host** (3DS player, Sunshine host PC): The player adds a host by LAN IP (host_discovery.cpp can also scan the network) and chooses pair; pair_host in src/n3ds_main.cpp shows a PIN to type into Sunshine and keeps a pair record.
- **Stream a game or desktop** (3DS player, Sunshine host PC): Video plays on the top screen using the New 3DS hardware H.264 decoder; older 3DS models fall back to software decode at lower frame rates, per the README.
- **Switch touch input modes** (3DS player, Sunshine host PC): The SELECT hub on the bottom screen switches between gamepad, mouse, keyboard, magnify and mirror handlers in src/input/touch/, plus Fit, Fill, Stretch and zoom display options.
- **Save performance as CSV** (3DS player): From the Session tab, the performance overlay shows stream telemetry; export_stream_benchmark_csv in src/stream_benchmark.cpp writes benchmark_&lt;time&gt;.csv to the SD card.
- **Build with devkitPro** (Developer): docker build of the Dockerfile gives a devkitPro image; make inside it produces artemis.3dsx, artemis.cia and artemis.elf. A local devkitPro 3ds-dev setup with bannertool and makerom also works.

### Scenario: Play a PC game on a New 3DS over Wi-Fi

1. Copy artemis.cia to the SD card and install it in FBI with Install and delete CIA.
2. Open Artemis, press A to add a host and enter the PC’s LAN IP address.
3. Choose pair and type the PIN shown on the 3DS into Sunshine’s PIN page.
4. Choose stream and pick an app; the video plays on the top screen.
5. Press SELECT to switch to Mouse or Magnify, or open the performance overlay and save a CSV.
6. Quit from the Session tab to end the stream.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| C&#43;&#43; | 76.05 |
| C | 15.71 |
| CMake | 4.36 |
| Makefile | 2.84 |
| Shell | 0.64 |
| Dockerfile | 0.4 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Docker (easiest)

```bash
docker build --network=host -t moonlight-n3ds .
docker run --rm -it -v .:/moonlight-N3DS -w /moonlight-N3DS moonlight-n3ds:latest
make
```

### README.md · Local (devkitPro)

```bash
make
```


## Features and components

- **Control plane** — n3ds_main.cpp brings together host discovery, pair records, profiles and connection state. The selected host and application determine the stream request. Graphics lifecycle state is tracked separately from stream configuration.
- **Media and interaction** — Audio, input and video live in separate src modules. Hardware capabilities influence the guidance shown to the user. The UI can return from a stream, while explicit system-close handling must unwind the application instead.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Host discovery and pairing → Selected app and profile
- Selected app and profile → GameStream connection
- GameStream connection → Video and audio backends
- Video and audio backends → 3DS screens and controls
- 3DS screens and controls → GameStream connection

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Host discovery and pairing&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Selected app and profile&#34;]
  n2[&#34;GameStream connection&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Video and audio backends&#34;]
  n4[&#34;3DS screens and controls&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
  n4 --&gt; n2
```

**One path through the code:** Follow SelectedHost and stream-profile selection before entering the media path. System close and a normal return to the menu are different transitions; the explicit close flag exists to keep those paths apart.

## Constraints and checks

The original and New 3DS have different decoding capabilities. Suggested presets in code are not measured guarantees of frame rate or network performance.

## Files to read

- [src/n3ds_main.cpp](https://github.com/antoinebou12/Artemis-N3DS/blob/n3ds-main/src/n3ds_main.cpp)
- [src/hardware_capabilities.cpp](https://github.com/antoinebou12/Artemis-N3DS/blob/n3ds-main/src/hardware_capabilities.cpp)
- [src/video/video.hpp](https://github.com/antoinebou12/Artemis-N3DS/blob/n3ds-main/src/video/video.hpp)

# Artemis-Switch: A streamed frame from host to screen

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/artemis-switch/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/artemis-switch/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/Artemis-Switch
- License: GPL-3.0
- Inspected revision: 33e6854781a47e86ae349e0a7646ff00bd924ddd

## Summary

Artemis-Switch is a fork in the Moonlight streaming family. The host runs the game. The client receives compressed video and audio, renders frames and sends controller input back.

**Why it exists:** Hardware-accelerated GameStream/Moonlight client in C&#43;&#43; with custom NVN display frame pacing for zero-stutter video.

**Best fit:** Ultra-low latency PC game streaming directly to Nintendo Switch handheld mode.

## Use cases

Moonlight-Switch fork that streams PC games to a Nintendo Switch, with FSR upscaling, stream profiles and telemetry.

- **Pair and stream from a host** (Switch player, GameStream host PC): GameStreamClient.cpp and MoonlightSession.cpp handle PIN pairing and sessions with Sunshine, Apollo, Vibeshine or Punktfunk; DiscoverManager finds hosts and WakeOnLanManager can wake them.
- **Tune video presentation** (Switch player): Fit, Fill, Stretch, Zoom/Pan, rotation and full range share one deko3d presentation path, with FSR/EASU upscaling, RCAS sharpening and dithering on top of NVDEC decode.
- **Save stream profiles** (Switch player, GameStream host PC): Named profiles store FPS (30 to 120), resolution, bitrate, codec and presentation in profile.json; they can be assigned per host, edited and imported or exported (StreamProfileStore.cpp, ProfileEditorDialog.cpp).
- **Export a benchmark** (Switch player): The Performance page shows bitrate, latency, frame queue, GPU time and Switch clocks; Benchmark start, stop and save write a file through app/src/benchmark/BenchmarkExport.cpp.
- **Build and test the app** (Developer): With devkitA64 and CMake, the Moonlight.nro target builds the Switch binary, exported by CI as Artemis-Switch.nro; tests/ holds portable unit tests run with ctest, plus Python i18n and release checks.

### Scenario: Stream a PC game to a Switch

1. Copy Artemis-Switch.nro to sdmc:/switch/Artemis-Switch/ and start hbmenu through title redirection.
2. Open Artemis Switch, select the PC host and finish PIN pairing in the host’s web UI.
3. Create a stream profile (for example 60 FPS, H.265, Fit with FSR) and assign it to that host.
4. Launch an app and press - and &#43; together to open the in-stream overlay.
5. Open Performance to watch bitrate and pipeline latency, then run and save a Benchmark.

## Features and components

- **Session and interface** — The Borealis interface handles host selection and settings. MoonlightSession coordinates streaming, while the Switch decoder-and-render provider chooses concrete video and audio implementations. UI state and media processing have different lifecycles.
- **Platform-specific output** — The provider constructs FFmpegVideoDecoder. With BOREALIS_USE_DEKO3D it selects ArtemisDKVideoRenderer, while other build flags select other renderers. Switch audio uses AudrenAudioRenderer. These are explicit build-time choices.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- GameStream host → Streaming session
- Streaming session → FFmpeg video decoder
- FFmpeg video decoder → deko3d renderer
- deko3d renderer → Switch display
- Controller input → Streaming session
- Streaming session → GameStream host

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;GameStream host&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Streaming session&#34;]
  n2[&#34;FFmpeg video decoder&#34;]
  n3[&#34;deko3d renderer&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Switch display&#34;]
  n5[&#34;Controller input&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
  n5 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n0
```

**One path through the code:** Read the provider methods to see which backend is actually compiled, then follow the session’s decoded frames into that renderer. Network, decode and presentation delays need separate measurements to explain a slow stream.

## Constraints and checks

A successful build does not establish hardware latency, codec support or stability on every target. Upstream Moonlight authorship remains credited.

# AudioTranscript: From WAV chunks to transcription

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/audiotranscript/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/audiotranscript/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/AudioTranscript
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 91b458e4385f0be729d8af54d8b500dc9d00a274

## Summary

AudioTranscript breaks a WAV recording into chunks around silence, sends each chunk to a recognition service and concatenates the results. The current implementation uses Amazon recognition, even though its docstrings still mention Google.

**Why it exists:** Audio ingestion and transcription worker pipeline with timestamp alignment.

**Best fit:** Batch automated audio recording transcription and indexing.

## Use cases

Python CLI that splits a WAV file on silence and transcribes each chunk into a single text.

- **Split audio on silence** (CLI user): main.py loads the WAV with pydub and calls split_on_silence with --min-silence-len, --silence-thresh (relative to the file’s dBFS) and --keep-silence, writing each piece to audio-chunks/chunkN.wav.
- **Transcribe the chunks** (CLI user, Amazon Transcribe): Each chunk goes to recognize_amazon (us-east-1, S3 bucket from .env) and the texts are joined and printed. The README describes Google Speech Recognition, but the code calls Amazon; the --language option is not passed on.
- **Set AWS keys in .env** (CLI user, Amazon Transcribe): load_dotenv reads AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_BUCKET_NAME; main.py raises an error if one is missing.
- **Try Whisper on a sample** (CLI user, Hugging Face Hub): ai.py is a separate script that loads openai/whisper-large-v2 with transformers and transcribes one LibriSpeech dummy sample; it is not wired to the CLI and its packages are not in requirements.txt.

### Scenario: Transcribe a recorded interview

1. Run pip install -r requirements.txt, plus python-dotenv, which main.py imports but the file does not list.
2. Create a .env file with AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_BUCKET_NAME.
3. Run python main.py interview.wav -m 700 -s -16 (the path is positional and defaults to caro.wav).
4. main.py writes the chunks to audio-chunks/ and shows a Rich progress bar.
5. Each chunk is sent to Amazon Transcribe and the full text is printed at the end.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 100 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Usage

```bash
python main.py --path &lt;audio_file_path&gt; --min-silence-len &lt;min_silence_length&gt; --silence-thresh &lt;silence_threshold&gt; --keep-silence &lt;keep_silence_duration&gt; --language &lt;language_code&gt;
```


## Features and components

- **Audio segmentation** — main.py loads a WAV through pydub and calls split_on_silence. The threshold is calculated relative to the recording’s dBFS level. Each chunk is exported to audio-chunks before recognition.
- **Recognition and output** — A SpeechRecognition Recognizer reads each exported file and calls recognize_amazon. The loop appends the returned text to whole_text, which is printed and returned. Typer exposes the file and segmentation parameters.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- WAV recording → pydub silence split
- pydub silence split → Temporary WAV chunks
- Temporary WAV chunks → Amazon recognition
- Amazon recognition → Combined text

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;WAV recording&#34;]
  n1[&#34;pydub silence split&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Temporary WAV chunks&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Amazon recognition&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Combined text&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Follow transcribe_audio_file rather than its docstring: the function checks AWS environment variables immediately before recognize_amazon. Its language argument is exposed by the CLI but is not passed into that call.

## Constraints and checks

Audio leaves the local machine for recognition. The code reuses fixed job and file names, so concurrent runs need separate naming and temporary-file handling.

- [requirements.txt](https://github.com/antoinebou12/AudioTranscript/blob/main/requirements.txt)

# AuthLaravel: Sessions, roles and Inertia pages

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/authlaravel/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/authlaravel/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/AuthLaravel
- Inspected revision: 2ec4e5d4367341fa789c0027d17ecd43ba80cf01

## Summary

AuthLaravel is an access-control learning project with a Laravel backend and Vue pages delivered through Inertia. The route definitions show how authenticated users reach their dashboard and how administrators receive a different view.

**Why it exists:** Clean Laravel authentication template implementing JWT, session management, and role-based policies.

**Best fit:** Secure boilerplate foundation for Laravel API and web applications.

## Use cases

Laravel 10 and React (Inertia) lab app for ÉTS GTI619 on roles, login throttling and password flows.

- **Register an account** (Registered user): RegisteredUserController stores a new user with email, username, phone and password; the form is resources/js/Pages/Auth/Register.tsx.
- **Log in with throttling** (Registered user, Administrator): LoginRequest locks an email and IP pair after 5 failed attempts and records login_attempts, browser, OS, IP and last_login on the user row.
- **Reset a forgotten password** (Registered user, Mailpit (dev mail)): The forgot-password routes send a reset link by email; in the Sail stack, Mailpit catches it and shows it on port 8025.
- **Change profile and password** (Registered user): PUT /password goes to PasswordController, and /profile lets the user edit, update or delete the account through ProfileController.
- **View all users as admin** (Administrator): /admin uses the AdminAuthenticated middleware, and /dashboard renders AdminDashboard.tsx with every user’s email, roles and permissions when the role is roles:admin; other roles get the plain dashboard.

### Scenario: Run the lab and test role-based access

1. From AuthLaravel/, run ./vendor/bin/sail up -d to start the app with MariaDB, Redis and Mailpit.
2. Run ./vendor/bin/sail artisan migrate and db:seed to create the admin, user, residential and business accounts.
3. Open http://localhost/login and sign in as admin@example.com to see the user table on the dashboard.
4. Sign in as user@example.com and open /admin; the middleware sends the user back to the dashboard.
5. Use Forgot password and read the reset email in Mailpit at http://localhost:8025.

# BatchBacktesting: comparable strategy runs

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/batchbacktesting/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/batchbacktesting/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/AlgoETS/BatchBacktesting
- Inspected revision: 6aae4af0733c248ae4c4dec1b25affa942f8037d


## Use cases

AlgoÉTS notebooks that backtest indicator strategies on S&amp;P 500 stocks and cryptos in parallel, with CSV and charts.

- **Build the ticker universe** (Strategy researcher, Wikipedia S&amp;P 500 list): get_SP500() reads the S&amp;P 500 symbol table from Wikipedia with pandas.read_html, and get_all_crypto() returns a fixed list of crypto pairs such as BTCUSD and ETHUSD.
- **Download daily prices** (Strategy researcher, FMP price API): process_instrument calls the FMP historical-price-full endpoint for stocks or the crypto variant, with FMP_API_KEY read from the environment in src/config.py.
- **Backtest one strategy in batch** (Strategy researcher, FMP price API): run_backtests(tickers, strategy=EMA, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True) runs backtesting.py on every ticker in a thread pool and writes output/raw/&lt;Strategy&gt;/&lt;ticker&gt;-&lt;start&gt;-&lt;end&gt;.csv.
- **Run all strategies on a ticker** (Strategy researcher): run_backtests_strategies([&#34;BMO&#34;], STRATEGIES_STR) submits every strategy defined in src/strategies.py (EMA, RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands, ADX, TRIX…) for the given instruments.
- **Compare returns to buy &amp; hold** (Strategy researcher): analyse.ipynb loads output/raw/&lt;Strategy&gt;/*.csv, ranks instruments by Return [%] and plots the top five against Buy &amp; Hold Return [%] with matplotlib.
- **Open the HTML trade charts** (Strategy researcher): With generate_plots=True, plot_results saves each backtesting.py chart as output/charts/&lt;Strategy&gt;/&lt;ticker&gt;-&lt;start&gt;-&lt;end&gt;.html; the repository already holds charts for 23 strategies.

### Scenario: Test EMA on the S&amp;P 500

1. Install the dependencies with pip install -r requirements.txt and put an FMP_API_KEY in the environment (see .env.exemple).
2. Run jupyter notebook and open batch.ipynb.
3. Run the cell tickers = get_SP500() then run_backtests(tickers, strategy=EMA, num_threads=12, generate_plots=True).
4. Check output/EMA-&lt;start&gt;-&lt;end&gt;.csv for the combined results and output/charts/EMA/ for one HTML chart per ticker.
5. Open analyse.ipynb and run the EMA section to list the top returns and compare them with buy and hold.

# bloc: Object storage inside Blender

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/bloc/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/bloc/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/bloc
- License: GPL-3.0
- Inspected revision: 6c83c217d541b632fdb0b8acc998c37e6f910075

## Summary

My bloc fork adds a Blender-facing workflow around S3 and MinIO storage. It preserves the upstream Blender-Cloud-Storage credit. The add-on translates object keys into a folder browser, then downloads assets before asking Blender to import them.

**Why it exists:** Direct AWS S3 object storage integration inside Blender via Boto3, eliminating local drive storage bloat for 3D assets.

**Best fit:** Cloud-native 3D asset synchronization, backup, and distributed rendering workflows.

## Use cases

Blender add-on that lists, uploads, downloads and imports files from MinIO or AWS S3 buckets in a sidebar panel.

- **Add a storage connection** (Blender user): In the add-on preferences, CloudConnection entries hold the type (MinIO or AWS S3), endpoint or region, access and secret keys and bucket name; several connections can be listed.
- **Browse and search the bucket** (Blender user, MinIO or S3 bucket): Refresh File List calls list_objects (MinIO) or list_objects_v2 (boto3) and draws a folder tree in the View3D Cloud tab; the Search field filters names by substring.
- **Upload the current .blend** (Blender user, MinIO or S3 bucket): Upload Current File sends the saved .blend under its file name. The README mentions uploading textures and other dependencies, but addon.py only uploads the .blend itself.
- **Import a mesh into the scene** (Blender user, MinIO or S3 bucket): Download saves an object to the system temp folder; Load to Scene downloads it and calls Blender’s STL, OBJ, USD or PLY importer.
- **Delete a remote file** (Blender user, MinIO or S3 bucket): Delete calls remove_object (MinIO) or delete_object (S3) and refreshes the list.

### Scenario: Pull a scan from a MinIO bucket into Blender

1. Install the add-on from Edit &gt; Preferences &gt; Add-ons; on first load it installs boto3, minio and rapidfuzz with pip.
2. In the preferences, add a MinIO connection with endpoint URL, keys and bucket name.
3. Open the Cloud tab in the 3D view sidebar and press Refresh File List.
4. Type part of a file name in Search to narrow the list.
5. Press Load to Scene on an .obj or .stl file to import it.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 100 |

## Features and components

- **Connection and listing** — CloudConnection stores provider, endpoint, bucket and region settings. The active connection determines the boto3 or MinIO client. Listing results are split on slashes to construct a nested dictionary for the panel.
- **Search and import** — CloudSearchManager scores names and path segments with RapidFuzz. A download first produces a temporary local file. The load operator then chooses an STL, OBJ, PLY or USD importer, so download success and import success remain separate states.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Blender panel → Active connection
- Active connection → S3 or MinIO API
- S3 or MinIO API → Object keys and folder tree
- Object keys and folder tree → Blender panel
- S3 or MinIO API → Temporary file
- Temporary file → Blender importer

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Blender panel&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Active connection&#34;]
  n2[&#34;S3 or MinIO API&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Object keys and folder tree&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Temporary file&#34;]
  n5[&#34;Blender importer&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n0
  n2 --&gt; n4
  n4 --&gt; n5
```

**One path through the code:** Follow refresh from object keys to the tree, then follow load from the selected key to a temporary path and an import operator. Background listing hands UI updates back through Blender timers. The stored object itself is not a local folder.

## Constraints and checks

The S3 path makes one list_objects_v2 request without pagination. Uploading the saved .blend file does not prove that external textures have been packaged.

## Files to read

- [addon.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/bloc/blob/main/addon.py)
- [blender_manifest.toml](https://github.com/antoinebou12/bloc/blob/main/blender_manifest.toml)

# ChitUI: A local bridge to resin printers

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/chitui/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/chitui/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/ChitUI
- Inspected revision: a4236172836c65116a88dcd39a934441691be34c

## Summary

ChitUI places a browser interface in front of SDCP resin printers. A Python process serves the web assets, discovers printers on the local network and translates browser actions into printer communication.

**Why it exists:** Full-featured web control interface for Chitubox SDCP 3.0 resin printers with LAN UDP discovery.

**Best fit:** Headless remote management and real-time print monitoring for SLA 3D printers.

## Use cases

Flask web UI that finds Chitubox SDCP 3.0 resin printers on the LAN, uploads files and starts prints.

- **Discover printers on the LAN** (Printer operator, SDCP resin printer): At start-up, discover_printers in main.py broadcasts M99999 over UDP port 3000, saves the replies and opens a WebSocket to each printer at ws://&lt;ip&gt;:3030/websocket.
- **Watch printer status** (Printer operator, SDCP resin printer): The browser asks over Socket.IO; main.py sends SDCP commands 0 (status) and 1 (attributes) and relays printer messages to web/js/chitui.js and sdcp.js.
- **Upload a print file** (Printer operator, SDCP resin printer): POST /upload accepts .ctb, .goo and .prz files, computes an MD5 and sends 1 MB parts to http://&lt;ip&gt;:3030/uploadFile/upload; /progress streams the percentage.
- **List and delete files** (Printer operator, SDCP resin printer): printer_files sends SDCP command 258 with a storage path; action_delete sends command 259 with the file list.
- **Start a print** (Printer operator, SDCP resin printer): action_print sends SDCP command 128 with the file name and StartLayer 0.

### Scenario: Send a sliced model to a resin printer from a browser

1. Install requirements.txt in a virtualenv and run python main.py, or use docker run --net=host so UDP broadcast works.
2. At start-up, ChitUI broadcasts M99999 on UDP port 3000 and connects to each printer’s WebSocket on port 3030.
3. Open http://127.0.0.1:54780/ to see the discovered printers and their status.
4. Upload a .ctb file; ChitUI saves it to /tmp and sends it in 1 MB parts with an MD5 check.
5. Pick the file in the printer’s file list and start the print.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| JavaScript | 48.61 |
| HTML | 24.57 |
| Python | 22.86 |
| CSS | 3.51 |
| Dockerfile | 0.45 |

## Verified technologies

- SDCP 3.0 — README title
- Docker — README Docker section
- Browser UI — README Usage, default port 54780
- Local network — README Docker host networking for UDP discovery

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Setup

```bash
python -mvenv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### README.md · Usage

```bash
python main.py
```


### Docker

```bash
docker build -t chitui:latest .
docker run --rm --name chitui --net=host chitui:latest
```

## Features and components

- **Browser and local server** — main.py builds a Flask application with web as its static folder and attaches Flask-SocketIO. Printer and WebSocket registries live in process memory. Discovery uses the local network, which explains the README’s Docker host-network requirement.
- **File transfer** — The upload route validates the extension and saves the incoming file temporarily. The printer upload helper calculates an MD5 checksum and sends one-megabyte parts with offsets. A separate event-stream route reports upload progress.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Browser UI → Flask and SocketIO
- Flask and SocketIO → Printer discovery and session
- Printer discovery and session → SDCP printer
- SDCP printer → Printer discovery and session

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Browser UI&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Flask and SocketIO&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Printer discovery and session&#34;]
  n3[&#34;SDCP printer&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n2
```

**One path through the code:** Follow /upload through the temporary file and the printer transfer helper. Transfer progress is global in this implementation, so simultaneous uploads would need per-job state to avoid mixing their percentages.

## Workflow

1. **Choose a file** — Select a supported print file for a discovered printer. The upload handler accepts multipart fields named file and printer.
2. **Validate the request** — The handler checks missing file or printer fields and the allowed extensions ctb, goo and prz before continuing.
3. **Store temporarily** — The server receives the file into temporary storage before starting transfer to the printer.
4. **Transfer to printer** — The helper sends chunks to the selected printer on the local network. Progress events are available on GET /progress as text/event-stream.
5. **Confirm the outcome** — Check the response and verify the file on the printer. The helper may report success after a failed part; treat the success body alone as incomplete proof of delivery.

## API


- `POST /upload`
- `GET /upload`
- `GET /progress`

## Constraints and checks

Treat this fork as a local-network prototype. A reachable web interface does not confirm compatibility with a particular printer firmware or safe remote access.

## Files to read

- [main.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ChitUI/blob/master/main.py)
- [Dockerfile](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ChitUI/blob/master/Dockerfile)
- [requirements.txt](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ChitUI/blob/master/requirements.txt)

# ComfyUI-UML: Diagram rendering inside a node graph

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/comfyui-uml/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/comfyui-uml/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/ComfyUI-UML
- Inspected revision: 1f1411580e0db67efd7a4ad669e42ba8677f546a

## Summary

ComfyUI-UML adds diagram-oriented nodes to ComfyUI. Text enters a workflow, a rendering backend turns it into an image, and the workflow can retain the source and viewer links alongside that output.

**Why it exists:** Custom node implementation for ComfyUI node graphs integrating automated UML synthesis into image pipelines.

**Best fit:** Visual AI workflows combining diagram generation with image refinement.

## Use cases

ComfyUI custom nodes that render Mermaid, PlantUML, Graphviz and other Kroki diagrams, optionally from LLM code.

- **Render a diagram from code** (ComfyUI user, Kroki API): The UML Render node (nodes/uml_diagram.py) sends code to Kroki through nodes/kroki_client.py and returns png, svg, jpeg, pdf, txt or base64, checked against each type’s supported formats.
- **Render Mermaid offline** (ComfyUI user): With backend set to local, web/js/render_mermaid.mjs uses beautiful-mermaid (after npm ci in web/js) to make SVG or PNG; Graphviz renders locally when the graphviz package is installed.
- **Generate code with an LLM** (ComfyUI user, LLM provider): UML Code Assistant (nodes/uml_llm.py), or LLM Prompt Engine followed by LLM Call, fills a template from prompts/ and calls Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini; the result feeds UML Render.
- **Preview and share a link** (ComfyUI user, Kroki API): Diagram Viewer URL (nodes/uml_viewer_url.py) turns kroki_url into a viewer link and an iframe link (viewer.html?embed=1) and shows a live preview in the node.
- **Save a diagram to ComfyUI** (ComfyUI user): The viewer’s Save button posts to /comfyui-uml/save, registered with the other routes in nodes/uml_routes.py.

### Scenario: Draw a sequence diagram from a prompt with a local Ollama model

1. Run comfy node install comfyui-uml (or clone into ComfyUI/custom_nodes and pip install -r requirements.txt), then restart ComfyUI.
2. Load workflows/uml_llm_ollama.json in the ComfyUI canvas.
3. Describe the diagram in UML Code Assistant, with provider ollama and a local model.
4. Queue the prompt; UML Render sends the generated code to Kroki and outputs the image.
5. Open the link from Diagram Viewer URL to zoom, copy the link or save the diagram to ComfyUI.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 50.91 |
| JavaScript | 45.75 |
| HTML | 3.34 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Installation

```bash
comfy node install comfyui-uml
```


## Features and components

- **Plugin registration** — The root __init__.py loads the nodes package under the unique name comfyui_uml_nodes. This avoids colliding with ComfyUI’s own nodes module. It exports the class mappings and the web directory used by the extension.
- **Rendering and viewer** — The nodes directory separates diagram generation, Kroki communication and viewer URLs. Browser assets are exposed through WEB_DIRECTORY, while route registration adds the viewer’s save-to-output integration. Local rendering options and Kroki are distinct backends.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Diagram text → Registered ComfyUI node
- Registered ComfyUI node → Local renderer
- Registered ComfyUI node → Kroki service
- Local renderer → Image and viewer links
- Kroki service → Image and viewer links

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Diagram text&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Registered ComfyUI node&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Local renderer&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Kroki service&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Image and viewer links&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n1 --&gt; n3
  n2 --&gt; n4
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Start at NODE_CLASS_MAPPINGS, then follow a diagram node into its renderer. The loader uses an explicit module specification because ComfyUI may import the plugin directly from a file path.

## Constraints and checks

Kroki rendering sends diagram text to the configured service. Use a suitable private endpoint for confidential diagrams and check which local renderer dependencies are installed.

- [nodes/uml_diagram.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ComfyUI-UML/blob/main/nodes/uml_diagram.py)
- [nodes/kroki_client.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ComfyUI-UML/blob/main/nodes/kroki_client.py)

# CV: One repository, several publishing paths

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/cv/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/cv/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/CV
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 2fdf469a3056498868554d59661713206d435b7b

## Summary

This website combines bilingual CV pages, structured resume data, LaTeX PDFs and a Hugo blog. A local script builds and validates both the CV and blog, then publishes them together from docs/ on main.

**Why it exists:** High-performance, accessible, bilingual static portfolio and CV with AEO schema, automated CI/CD, and zero runtime overhead.

**Best fit:** Professional software engineering presentation and technical documentation.

## Use cases

Source of antoineboucher.info/CV: bilingual HTML CV, LaTeX PDFs, JSON résumé and a Hugo blog with project pages.

- **Update CV content** (Site owner): The owner edits index-en.html and index-fr.html, data/resume.*.json and data/cv.yaml; scripts/build/generate_cv.py writes the LaTeX skills.tex files from the YAML.
- **Build the PDF résumés** (Site owner): python build_cv.py build --all compiles cv-en/resume.tex and cv-fr/resume.tex with XeLaTeX inside a Docker image.
- **Refresh project pages** (Site owner): scripts/build/repository_docs.py reads public repositories without running their code and writes hugo/data/repository_*.json, which the repository-note shortcode renders under hugo/content/projects/notes/&lt;slug&gt;/.
- **Publish the site** (Site owner, GitHub Pages): scripts/deploy/publish_site.py runs build_docs.py (Hugo with HUGO_ENV=production, sitemap merge, deploy checks), check_public_repos.py and the note tests, then with --publish commits docs/ and pushes main.
- **Read the CV in EN or FR** (Recruiter or reader, GitHub Pages): GitHub Pages serves /CV/index-en.html and /CV/index-fr.html, the PDFs under /CV/cv-en/ and /CV/cv-fr/, and /CV/resume.json or /CV/resume.md for machine reading.
- **Browse blog and projects** (Recruiter or reader, GitHub Pages): The Hugo build is published at /CV/blog/ and /CV/blog/fr/, with a Markdown twin of each page and llms.txt, robots.txt and sitemap.xml copied to the site root.

### Scenario: Ship a CV update

1. Edit the job entry in index-en.html and index-fr.html and the matching data/resume.en.json and data/resume.fr.json.
2. Run python build_cv.py build --all to rebuild cv-en/resume.pdf and cv-fr/resume.pdf.
3. Run python scripts/deploy/publish_site.py to build the CV and blog into a staging folder, validate it and update docs/.
4. Review docs/ locally, commit the source changes, then rerun the script with --publish to commit docs/ and push main.
5. Wait for GitHub Pages (main, /docs) to process the push and check https://antoineboucher.info/CV/.

## Features and components

- **Assembly and verification** — build_docs.py stages the root pages and assets, builds Hugo under the blog path, merges the root sitemap and runs deployment verification before copying the output to docs. Staging keeps a failed build from overwriting that published tree.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Resume JSON and AEO data → Generated resume and About

# D2COpenAIPlugin: Routing text to diagram backends

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/d2copenaiplugin/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/d2copenaiplugin/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/D2COpenAIPlugin
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 7d15ee155d5f392b1d90192dc2e21ec479a6291a

## Summary

D2COpenAIPlugin is a FastAPI diagram service with a plugin manifest and an OpenAPI surface. Its implementation selects among PlantUML, Mermaid and Kroki paths based on the request’s diagram language.

**Why it exists:** OpenAI ChatGPT plugin manifest and OpenAPI endpoint handler for text-to-diagram conversion.

**Best fit:** ChatGPT Plus GPT Store integration for software architects.

## Use cases

FastAPI ChatGPT-plugin backend that turns PlantUML, Mermaid, D2 or Kroki source into diagram links.

- **Get a PlantUML image link** (ChatGPT plugin client, Diagram renderers): POST /generate_diagram with lang plantuml encodes the code for the public PlantUML server (theme blueprint by default) and returns url, content and playground.
- **Open Mermaid in Live Editor** (ChatGPT plugin client, Diagram renderers): For lang mermaid, mermaid/mermaid.py builds an encoded editor state (theme dark by default) and returns Mermaid Live Editor links.
- **Render D2 or Kroki types** (ChatGPT plugin client, Diagram renderers): D2 aliases and every language in KROKI_LANGUAGE_SUPPORT go through generate_kroki_diagram in kroki/kroki.py and return an SVG link.
- **Serve the plugin manifest** (ChatGPT plugin client): app.py serves /.well-known/ai-plugin.json, /openapi.yaml, /openapi.json, /logo.png and /.well-known/privacy.txt so a ChatGPT client can load the plugin.
- **Run and test locally** (Developer): uvicorn app:app serves the API on port 5003 with docs at /; test_app.py covers the endpoints in CI, and vercel.json routes every path to app.py.

### Scenario: Connect the plugin to ChatGPT on localhost

1. Create a virtualenv, run pip install -r requirements-dev.txt and python -m pytest.
2. Start the API with uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5003.
3. In ChatGPT, choose Develop your own plugin and enter localhost:5003 to load /.well-known/ai-plugin.json.
4. Ask for a sequence diagram; ChatGPT calls POST /generate_diagram with lang plantuml.
5. The API returns the image URL and a playground link that ChatGPT shows to the user.

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 100 |





```bash

```

### plantuml/README.md · Installation

```bash

```

### plantuml/README.md · Command Line Usage

```bash
usage: plantuml.py [-h] [-o OUT] [-s SERVER] filename [filename ...]
Generate images from PlantUML defined files using PlantUML server
positional arguments: 
  filename            file(s) to generate images from
optional arguments: 
  -h, --help          show this help message and exit 
  -o OUT, --out OUT   directory to put the files into 
  -s SERVER, --server SERVER 
                      server to generate from; defaults to plantuml.com 
```


## Features and components

- **Request model** — DiagramRequest contains lang, type, code and theme. Validators check the language and source length. /generate_diagram rejects missing fields before dispatching to a backend; the code then builds result and playground links.
- **Backend adapters** — PlantUML uses its dedicated client, Mermaid builds an editor state, and D2 aliases are normalized to the Kroki d2 renderer. Other supported languages use the Kroki language registry. The adapters isolate differing URL and encoding conventions.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Structured diagram request → FastAPI model and route
- FastAPI model and route → PlantUML adapter
- FastAPI model and route → Mermaid state encoder
- FastAPI model and route → Kroki adapter
- PlantUML adapter → Result and playground links
- Mermaid state encoder → Result and playground links
- Kroki adapter → Result and playground links

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Structured diagram request&#34;]
  n1[&#34;FastAPI model and route&#34;]
  n2[&#34;PlantUML adapter&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Mermaid state encoder&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Kroki adapter&#34;]
  n5[&#34;Result and playground links&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n1 --&gt; n3
  n1 --&gt; n4
  n2 --&gt; n5
  n3 --&gt; n5
  n4 --&gt; n5
```

**One path through the code:** Compare the PlantUML and D2 branches in app.py. They accept the same request model but use different rendering adapters. The type validator logs an invalid type rather than raising, so it is not equivalent to strict language validation.

## Constraints and checks

The plugin manifest documents the original integration format. Its presence does not establish current availability in a third-party product or confidentiality of remote rendering.

# DasherControl: A workspace dashboard across three boundaries

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/dashercontrol/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/dashercontrol/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/DasherControl
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: d5e4b5af44ce8a19025fd41569978f9a3b1b910d

## Summary

DasherControl brings homelab links and embedded applications into saved workspaces. Vue handles the interface, Rust and Rocket expose the API, and Diesel persists the layout in PostgreSQL. Docker control follows a separate path.

**Why it exists:** Decoupled homelab architecture: Rust/Rocket backend managing Docker daemon via Shiplift, paired with a reactive Vue workspace frontend.

**Best fit:** Centralized command dashboard for homelab containerized services, bookmarks, and layout management.

## Use cases

Rust (Rocket) and Vue dashboard for a home lab: grid workspaces of applets plus basic Docker container control.

- **Sign in to the dashboard** (Homelab admin, PostgreSQL): cargo run --bin create_admin creates the first account; POST /tenants/api/login checks the bcrypt hash and returns a JWT used by the protected routes.
- **Arrange applets in a grid** (Homelab admin): GridLayoutMain.vue places applets such as IFrame, Shortcut, Editor, Canvas, Terminal and DockerManager on a resizable grid.
- **Save and switch workspaces** (Homelab admin, PostgreSQL): The /workspaces/api routes create, update, list and delete workspaces and their applets, stored in PostgreSQL through Diesel.
- **Stop or restart containers** (Homelab admin, Docker Engine): /containers/api/docker_list lists containers through shiplift, and /containers/api/stop/&lt;id&gt; and restart/&lt;id&gt; act on one container when a valid token is sent.
- **Open a web SSH terminal** (Homelab admin): src/bin/start_websocket.rs bridges a WebSocket to an ssh2 session for the Terminal applet; the README lists the web terminal as in progress.

### Scenario: Set up the dashboard on an Ubuntu server

1. Build the frontend with cd frontend &amp;&amp; npm install &amp;&amp; npm run build.
2. Set DATABASE_URL in Rocket.toml and .env, then run diesel migration run.
3. Run cargo run --bin create_admin, then cargo run to start the Rocket server.
4. Sign in, add IFrame applets for services such as Sonarr or Jellyfin and save the workspace.
5. Open the DockerManager applet to list containers and restart one.

| --- | ---: |

```bash
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker-compose up -d --build &amp;&amp; docker-compose logs -f
```

## Features and components

- **Workspace ownership** — Workspace list handlers derive a tenant identifier from a token. The applet retrieval handler checks the workspace’s tenant before returning its contents. A workspace and its applets therefore form a persisted user-owned layout.
- **Container operations** — src/containers/docker.rs wraps Shiplift operations for Docker. These calls manage containers and images rather than layout records. Their failure handling matters: a failed list request prints an error and returns an empty vector.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Vue workspace UI → Rocket handlers
- Rocket handlers → Diesel and PostgreSQL
- Rocket handlers → Shiplift adapter
- Shiplift adapter → Docker daemon

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Vue workspace UI&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Rocket handlers&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Diesel and PostgreSQL&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Shiplift adapter&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Docker daemon&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n1 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Loading a workspace reaches the tenant-aware handlers and then its applet records. Restarting a container goes through the Docker adapter instead. The UI should distinguish an empty workspace, an unavailable Docker service and an iframe blocked by the embedded application.

## Compose services

| Service | Runtime | Ports | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dashercontrol | Build from multi-stage Dockerfile | 8000:8000 | postgres, startup healthcheck |
| postgres | postgres:14-alpine | 5432:5432 |  |

## Constraints and checks

Older create and delete routes use different authorization checks. This prototype needs an operation-by-operation authorization review before shared deployment.

# Dimension: From matrix storage to a rendered scene

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/dimension/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/dimension/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/Dimension
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 5281d0932aa99ea0d2c43e64c388b9256c75b126

## Summary

Dimension is my Rust workspace for mathematics and graphics experiments. mathlib provides numerical building blocks; render uses them for CPU-side transforms and cameras before submitting graphics work through wgpu.

**Why it exists:** High-performance wgpu graphics pipeline and linear algebra math engine built entirely in Rust from first principles.

**Best fit:** Hardware-accelerated 3D heightmap rendering, spatial transformation pipelines, and graphics education.

## Use cases

A Rust workspace around mathlib: linear algebra, wgpu rendering, parsers, physics and geometry, with WASM demos.

- **Compute with dense and sparse** (Rust developer): The mathlib crate provides dense and sparse matrices, vectors, SVD and 3D helpers; cd mathlib &amp;&amp; cargo test and cargo bench exercise them.
- **Render a 3D scene with wgpu** (Rust developer, GPU via wgpu): The render crate draws a mathlib Tree scene through wgpu; cargo run -p render-demo --example render_native opens a window with a cube, gizmo and picking.
- **Load meshes and data files** (Rust developer): The parse crate reads JSON, XML, OBJ, MTL, BVH, glTF, PLY, PNG, JPEG, ZIP and TAR behind Cargo features such as json and obj.
- **Simulate physics, collisions** (Rust developer): physics implements PBD/XPBD with examples particles_2d, rigid_bodies_3d and softbody_3d; collision adds AABB, OBB, BVH, BSP, ray and frustum queries.
- **Publish the WASM demo site** (Rust developer, Browser (WASM/WebGPU)): just website-build compiles the mathlib, render, kinematics, physics, geometry and neural demos to WASM into website/; pages.yml deploys it to GitHub Pages.

### Scenario: Trying the demos locally before a push

1. Run cd mathlib &amp;&amp; cargo test to check the core library.
2. Run just run-render to open the native wgpu scene and move the gizmo.
3. Run just website-build to compile every demo to WASM into website/.
4. Run just website-serve and open http://localhost:3000/ to browse /mathlib/, /render/ and /physics/.
5. Push to main; the Pages workflow rebuilds website/ and publishes it.

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Rust | 63.95 |

| Just | 0.52 |
| CSS | 0.51 |
| WGSL | 0.4 |

## Features and components

- **Data and numerical operations** — mathlib exports dense and sparse storage, matrix views, vectors and numerical methods. A caller chooses the representation that fits its problem. Optional executor features are separate from the basic storage API.
- **Scene and platform boundary** — render exports World, EntityId and Transform, with parent-child scene relationships. Native windowing and WebAssembly canvas support sit around the renderer. The root workspace also contains geometry, collision, kinematics and physics crates.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Application or demo → mathlib data and transforms
- mathlib data and transforms → Scene hierarchy and camera
- Scene hierarchy and camera → wgpu resources and passes
- wgpu resources and passes → Native window or web canvas

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Application or demo&#34;]
  n1[&#34;mathlib data and transforms&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Scene hierarchy and camera&#34;]
  n3[&#34;wgpu resources and passes&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Native window or web canvas&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** For a scene update, start with a local Transform and its parent relationship. Follow the scene representation toward the renderer rather than assuming a matrix calculation executes on the GPU. wgpu is the graphics backend; mathlib’s optional GPU executor is a different feature.

## Constraints and checks

Workspace membership shows available modules, not a completed physics engine or measured performance. Benchmarks need a specified workload, feature set and target device.

# donneesqc-mcp: An MCP gateway to public data

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/donneesqc-mcp/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/donneesqc-mcp/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/donneesqc-mcp
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 53a6ee4209c44ccfe360556a1b86c29d855f3e2f

## Summary

donneesqc-mcp is a fork exposing Québec and Montréal open-data operations through MCP tools. Its entry point registers the tool collection and starts an HTTP transport, leaving dataset access and geographic helpers in separate modules.

**Why it exists:** Production MCP server connecting AI assistants to Quebec &amp; Montreal open data APIs with strict schema validation.

**Best fit:** Natural language querying of public municipal and provincial datasets across transportation, demographics, and municipal services.

## Use cases

An MCP server that lets AI agents search, query in SQL and map Québec and Montréal open data in conversation.

- **Search open datasets** (Analyst with an agent, CKAN open data portals): search_datasets and search_montreal_datasets call the CKAN APIs of Données Québec and Montréal (DQ_API_URL, MTL_API_URL) through helpers/ckan_api.py.
- **Run read-only SQL queries** (Analyst with an agent, CKAN open data portals): query_resource_sql and query_montreal_sql send SQL to the CKAN DataStore after validate_sql() rejects anything that is not a SELECT.
- **Find and query in one call** (Analyst with an agent, CKAN open data portals): find_and_query chains search, resource listing and DataStore query so the agent avoids three round trips.
- **Explore geospatial layers** (Analyst with an agent, IGO geo services): list_geospatial_layers, get_geospatial_features and get_map_url query the IGO WFS and build WMS GetMap URLs through helpers/geo_api.py.
- **Geocode, convert coordinates** (Analyst with an agent, IGO geo services): geocode and reverse_geocode use the icherche geocoder (GEOCODER_URL); convert_coordinates switches between EPSG:32198 and EPSG:4326.

### Scenario: Counting public trees per borough in Montréal

1. Start the server with docker compose up -d (or uv sync then uv run python main.py); it listens on port 8000 with streamable HTTP.
2. Register it in the client, for example claude mcp add --transport http donneesqc http://localhost:8000/mcp.
3. Ask the agent for public tree data; it calls search_montreal_datasets to find the dataset.
4. The agent calls query_montreal_data to see the columns of the DataStore resource.
5. It sends a SELECT … GROUP BY query through query_montreal_sql and answers with the per-borough counts.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 98.28 |
| Shell | 1.36 |
| Dockerfile | 0.36 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Installation manuelle

```bash

cd donneesqc-mcp
uv sync
cp .env.example .env
set -a &amp;&amp; source .env &amp;&amp; set &#43;a
uv run python main.py
```

### README.md · Quick start

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Stefen-Taime/donneesqc-mcp.git
cd donneesqc-mcp
docker compose up -d
```


## Features and components

- **Server bootstrap** — main.py configures logging, optionally initializes Sentry, calls register_all_tools and runs the MCP object with streamable-http. Monitoring is optional; it is not the mechanism that serves dataset queries.
- **Data-service boundary** — The documented tool groups cover catalog discovery, CKAN DataStore access, resource downloads and geographic enrichment. A catalog result describes a resource; the actual table or file is a separate request and may use a different format.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- MCP client → Registered HTTP tools
- Registered HTTP tools → Catalog search
- Catalog search → Table or file resource
- Table or file resource → Structured result
- Structured result → MCP client

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;MCP client&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Registered HTTP tools&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Catalog search&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Table or file resource&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Structured result&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
  n4 --&gt; n0
```

**One path through the code:** Follow main into register_all_tools, then choose the dataset-access tool behind a catalog result. Resource identifiers, formats and geographic coordinate systems matter more than a dataset title alone.

## Constraints and checks

Open-data catalogs and schemas can change. A successful catalog query does not prove that every resource is fresh, complete or compatible with a downstream calculation.

# ESP32-7SEG: An embedded clock with network setup

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/esp32-7seg/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/esp32-7seg/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/ESP32-7SEG
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 6cac20eed8dc6293d011a0c8a8341654e0870b80

## Summary

ESP32-7SEG connects an ESP32 clock display to network configuration and an HTTP interface. The firmware startup decides whether saved Wi-Fi settings can be reused or whether the device needs its setup path.

**Why it exists:** Embedded microcontroller firmware and mobile controller for driving multi-digit 7-segment displays.

**Best fit:** Physical computing status dashboards and hardware displays.

## Use cases

ESP32 firmware and an Android app that drive an I2C 7-segment display as a countdown or stopwatch over Wi-Fi.

- **Join the board to Wi-Fi** (Timer operator, ESP32 &#43; 7-seg display): Without saved credentials, wifi.cpp starts an access point named ESPTimer; the / page then serves the setup form, and POST /connect stores the SSID and password in NVS.
- **Start a countdown or stopwatch** (Timer operator, ESP32 &#43; 7-seg display): POST /timer-action with action, mode, minutes and seconds starts, pauses or stops a FreeRTOS task (COUNTDOWN or STOPWATCH) in display.cpp.
- **Set the digits directly** (Timer operator, ESP32 &#43; 7-seg display): POST /update-display with minutes and seconds calls updateDisplay() and pushes a displayUpdated message.
- **Follow updates live** (Android app, ESP32 &#43; 7-seg display): The /ws WebSocket broadcasts timerStarted, timerStopped and displayUpdated JSON; the Android WebSocketClient listens to it.
- **Control it from Android** (Timer operator, Android app): TimerApiService.kt maps the same endpoints with Retrofit (/timer-action, /connect, /scan, /update-display, /device-info) behind the TimerControl and WiFiConnect fragments.

### Scenario: Setting up a 5-minute countdown on a fresh board

1. Wire the Adafruit I2C backpack to SDA, SCL, VCC and GND, then flash the firmware with pio run -t upload (env firebeetle).
2. On first boot no credentials are in NVS, so join the ESPTimer access point and open the board&#39;s page.
3. Pick a network from /scan and submit it to /connect; the board saves it and joins the LAN.
4. Read the new IP in the serial monitor at 115200 baud and open it in a browser or the Android app.
5. Send action=start, mode=countdown, minutes=5, seconds=0 to /timer-action; the display counts down and /ws reports each update.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Kotlin | 58.26 |
| C&#43;&#43; | 39.56 |
| C | 2.18 |

## Features and components

- **Boot and connectivity** — setup initializes NVS and checks its result. It loads saved credentials, attempts a connection and falls back to setupWiFi if needed. The same fallback runs when no saved credentials exist.
- **Display and web modules** — After connectivity setup, main.cpp calls startClockDisplay and setupWebServer. display.cpp, wifi.cpp and web_server.cpp keep hardware display, connection management and HTTP handling in separate modules.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- ESP32 boot → NVS saved settings
- NVS saved settings → Connect or setup Wi-Fi
- Connect or setup Wi-Fi → Clock display
- Connect or setup Wi-Fi → HTTP interface

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;ESP32 boot&#34;]
  n1[&#34;NVS saved settings&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Connect or setup Wi-Fi&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Clock display&#34;]
  n4[&#34;HTTP interface&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n2 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Follow the saved-credentials branch in setup. A stored network is attempted first, but failure still reaches setupWiFi. Only after that branch does the code start the display and web server.

## Constraints and checks

Hardware wiring, display support and Wi-Fi setup must be checked on the device. This HTTP interface should not be assumed safe for unrestricted Internet exposure.

## Files to read

- [src/main.cpp](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ESP32-7SEG/blob/main/src/main.cpp)
- [src/display.cpp](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ESP32-7SEG/blob/main/src/display.cpp)
- [src/web_server.cpp](https://github.com/antoinebou12/ESP32-7SEG/blob/main/src/web_server.cpp)
