# FlashGames: A static shell around a Flash runtime

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/flashgames/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/flashgames/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/FlashGames
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 7ee14ee2c3029c3b797d22f7594d04c4c900441c

## Summary

FlashGames preserves small Flash games in a browser-facing collection. The page selects a SWF and hosts the Ruffle player. The game binary and the surrounding HTML interface remain separate pieces.

**Why it exists:** Preservation archive of early 2010s ActionScript/Flash game creations with self-contained assets.

**Best fit:** Digital preservation and retro gaming nostalgia.

## Use cases

A browser page that replays three Flash games from 2010 through the Ruffle emulator, with no plugin needed.

- **Pick a game from the list** (Player): The #swfSelector drop-down in index.html lists Tag, Ricochet Kill and Ballon, each with a short description.
- **Play a SWF in the browser** (Player, Ruffle emulator): loadSWF() creates a Ruffle player with RufflePlayer.newest() and loads tag.swf, ricochet kill.swf or jeux.swf into #swfContainer.
- **Open a game by URL hash** (Player): updateHash() writes the game key into the URL hash, and the load and hashchange listeners reload that game, so a link like #tag opens it directly.
- **Run the collection locally** (Player, Ruffle emulator): The README says to clone the repository and open index.html; Ruffle is loaded from unpkg, so a network connection is still needed.

### Scenario: Replaying Ricochet Kill from a shared link

1. Open https://antoinebou12.github.io/FlashGames/ (or index.html from a clone).
2. The page loads the first game, Tag, because no hash is set.
3. Choose Ricochet Kill in the Select a Game list; the URL becomes #ricochet_kill.
4. Ruffle loads ricochet kill.swf into the black game area and the description bar updates.
5. Play with the mouse, then copy the URL to send someone straight to the same game.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| HTML | 100 |

## Features and components

- **Selection and runtime** — index.html includes the Ruffle script, a game selector and a player container. Selection updates the page state before loading the chosen SWF. Styles and icons come from CDN assets rather than a local frontend build.
- **Preserved game files** — The repository stores the SWF files alongside the page. Ruffle supplies the browser-compatible execution layer; the page does not rewrite the games into JavaScript source.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Game selector → Static page state
- Static page state → Ruffle player
- Selected SWF → Ruffle player

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Game selector&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Static page state&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Ruffle player&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Selected SWF&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n3 --&gt; n2
```

**One path through the code:** Trace the selector’s updateHash handler toward the player container. This is a useful distinction when debugging: a selector problem belongs to the page, while unsupported game behavior may belong to the runtime.

## Constraints and checks

Runtime compatibility must be checked per game. External scripts also affect availability even though the page itself is static.

# GithubSimpleFileDownloader: A browser extension tied to page structure

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/githubsimplefiledownloader/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/githubsimplefiledownloader/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/GithubSimpleFileDownloader
- Inspected revision: dfdd7966db41841e272eddfeefe80332feab161d

## Summary

This archived extension attempted to add individual-file download controls to repository browsers. Its GitHub implementation shows the fragility of building an integration around another website’s DOM rather than a stable application interface.

**Why it exists:** Browser extension injecting one-click raw file download buttons into GitHub &amp; GitLab interfaces.

**Best fit:** Quick single-file extraction without cloning large repositories.

## Use cases

A Chrome extension that adds a download link and file size next to each file in GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket listings.

- **Add icons to file listings** (Repository visitor, Git hosting site): manifest.json injects inject_github.js, inject_gitlab.js or inject_bitbucket.js on matching pages; each script appends an icon link to every row (td.content, td.tree-item-file-name or tr.iterable-item).
- **Download a single file** (Repository visitor, Git hosting site): The script rewrites the blob link to its raw URL (raw.githubusercontent.com on GitHub, /raw/ on GitLab), fetches the text and sets a Blob object URL with a download attribute.
- **Show each file&#39;s size** (Repository visitor, Git hosting site): On GitHub, getFileURLDocument() loads the file page with XMLHttpRequest and changeFileSize() copies the Bytes/KB/MB line into a span next to the icon.
- **Open a folder from its icon** (Repository visitor, Git hosting site): Paths without a file extension are treated as directories, so the icon simply links to the folder page instead of downloading.

### Scenario: Grabbing one config file from a GitHub repository

1. Load the extension in Chrome (Manifest V2, content scripts for github.com, gitlab.com and bitbucket.org).
2. Open a repository&#39;s file list on github.com; inject_github.js waits for document.readyState to be complete.
3. A small GitHub icon and a size label appear next to each file row.
4. Click the icon next to the file: the raw content is saved under the file&#39;s name.
5. If icons do not appear, refresh the page as the README advises; the README title also flags the extension as not working.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| JavaScript | 97.74 |
| CSS | 2.26 |

## Features and components

- **Content-script injection** — The GitHub script waits for document readiness, locates td.content cells and inserts icons, links and size labels. Separate scripts target GitLab and Bitbucket. Each adapter depends on that site’s markup.
- **Raw-file download** — The script converts a repository file link to a raw URL, fetches text and creates a Blob download link. Its text-based path should not be assumed to preserve arbitrary binary files.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Repository web page → Injected content script
- Injected content script → DOM link extraction
- DOM link extraction → Raw file request
- Raw file request → Blob download link

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Repository web page&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Injected content script&#34;]
  n2[&#34;DOM link extraction&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Raw file request&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Blob download link&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Start at querySelectorAll(&#39;td.content&#39;) and inspect how child-node positions select the original link. A changed table layout can break this path before the network request is even made.

## Constraints and checks

The README explicitly marks the extension as not working. This is a historical implementation, not a current download recommendation.

## Files to read

- [manifest.json](https://github.com/antoinebou12/GithubSimpleFileDownloader/blob/master/manifest.json)
- [src/inject/inject_github.js](https://github.com/antoinebou12/GithubSimpleFileDownloader/blob/master/src/inject/inject_github.js)
- [src/inject/inject_gitlab.js](https://github.com/antoinebou12/GithubSimpleFileDownloader/blob/master/src/inject/inject_gitlab.js)

# GreenScreenVideotoAlphaPNGs: A transparent-frame production pipeline

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/greenscreenvideotoalphapngs/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/greenscreenvideotoalphapngs/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/GreenScreenVideotoAlphaPNGs
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: b487e51f3c702aee2b21f0149727c3cb2708f09a

## Summary

GreenScreenVideotoAlphaPNGs separates video acquisition, frame extraction and chroma keying from final encoding. RGBA PNG frames are an intermediate output that can feed either the GIF path or an alpha-capable video codec.

**Why it exists:** OpenCV color-keying pipeline converting chroma-key green videos to RGBA alpha PNG sequences.

**Best fit:** Asset preparation for augmented reality (Snapchat Lens Studio, Spark AR).

## Use cases

A Python CLI that turns green-screen video into transparent PNG frames, GIFs or alpha .mov files for Lens Studio.

- **Download footage from a URL** (AR lens creator, YouTube (yt-dlp)): greenscreen convert accepts a YouTube URL; convert.py calls download_video() and download_audio() from download.py, which use yt-dlp.
- **Split a video into frames** (AR lens creator, ffmpeg): frames.py writes numbered PNGs (0.png, 1.png…) with ffmpeg, or with OpenCV when --no-ffmpeg is passed.
- **Key out the green background** (AR lens creator): chroma.py computes a YCbCr distance from the key color (pixel 1,1 by default, tolerance 50–130) and writes RGBA PNGs into a sibling *_alpha folder.
- **Build a transparent GIF** (AR lens creator, ffmpeg): greenscreen gif &lt;dir&gt; uses numpngw and the optional APNGLib extension by default, or an ffmpeg palette with --fast-ffmpeg; the GIF is written next to the folder.
- **Encode an alpha .mov** (AR lens creator, ffmpeg): greenscreen video &lt;dir&gt; --fps 30 encodes the PNG sequence to Videogen-&lt;stamp&gt;.mov with the qtrle or prores_4444 codec.

### Scenario: From a green-screen clip to a Lens Studio animation

1. Run bash install.sh (or .\install.ps1 on Windows), then uv run greenscreen --help.
2. Run uv run greenscreen convert clip.mp4 to extract frames into clip/ and keyed frames into clip_alpha/.
3. Outputs that start with the clip name are moved into project_clip/ unless --no-project-dir is set.
4. Run uv run greenscreen gif project_clip/clip_alpha --fast-ffmpeg to get a transparent GIF without APNGLib.
5. In Lens Studio, use Resources → Add New → 2D animation from files and pick the *_alpha PNGs.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| C&#43;&#43; | 57.96 |
| Python | 32.32 |
| JavaScript | 7.93 |
| PowerShell | 0.94 |
| Shell | 0.85 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Quick start (uv)

```bash
.\install.ps1
uv run greenscreen --help
```

### README.md · Quick start (uv)

```bash
bash install.sh
uv run greenscreen --help
```

### README.md · APNGLib (optional C&#43;&#43; extension)

```bash
$env:SKIP_APNGLIB=&#39;1&#39;; uv sync --extra dev
```

### README.md · APNGLib (optional C&#43;&#43; extension)

```bash
$env:SKIP_APNGLIB=&#39;0&#39;; uv sync --extra dev
```


## Features and components

- **Conversion stage** — The Typer convert command delegates to run_convert. It accepts a local video or URL and can prefer FFmpeg or force OpenCV extraction. The chroma module handles pixel transparency separately from acquisition.
- **Encoding choices** — gif and video take a directory of PNG frames. The GIF path offers an FFmpeg palette option; video accepts qtrle or prores_4444. Encoding is a new stage, so frame rate and format can change without repeating acquisition.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Video file or URL → Frame extraction
- Frame extraction → Chroma key
- Chroma key → RGBA PNG sequence
- RGBA PNG sequence → GIF encoder
- RGBA PNG sequence → Alpha video encoder

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Video file or URL&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Frame extraction&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Chroma key&#34;]
  n3[&#34;RGBA PNG sequence&#34;]
  n4[&#34;GIF encoder&#34;]
  n5[&#34;Alpha video encoder&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
  n3 --&gt; n5
```

**One path through the code:** Follow cmd_convert into run_convert, then reuse its PNG output for cmd_video. Preserving the intermediate frames makes it easier to inspect matte edges before compression obscures them.

## Constraints and checks

Codec availability depends on the installed FFmpeg build. GIF transparency and video alpha have different capabilities and should not be treated as equivalent.

## Files to read

- [src/greenscreen/cli.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/GreenScreenVideotoAlphaPNGs/blob/master/src/greenscreen/cli.py)
- [src/greenscreen/chroma.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/GreenScreenVideotoAlphaPNGs/blob/master/src/greenscreen/chroma.py)
- [src/greenscreen/video_pipeline.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/GreenScreenVideotoAlphaPNGs/blob/master/src/greenscreen/video_pipeline.py)

# hass_renpho: Polling a cloud API into Home Assistant sensors

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/hass-renpho/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/hass-renpho/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/hass_renpho
- Inspected revision: b38c9dfa5416e5c1d09619d963b7bfaac238494b

## Summary

hass_renpho is a fork of a Home Assistant integration for Renpho measurements. A shared coordinator refreshes cloud data and sensor entities expose that state. The repository warns that its old-app API path is no longer reliably working.

**Why it exists:** Custom Home Assistant integration decoding Renpho Bluetooth &amp; Cloud API biometric telemetry.

**Best fit:** Self-hosted health metric tracking and smart home automation triggers.

## Use cases

A Home Assistant integration that polls the legacy Renpho cloud API and exposes scale measurements as sensors.

- **Sign in and pick a scale user** (Home Assistant user, Home Assistant, Renpho cloud API): config_flow.py validates the email and password against Renpho, then shows a select_user step when the account has several scale users.
- **Poll measurements on a timer** (Home Assistant, Renpho cloud API): RenphoWeightCoordinator calls get_measurements(), list_girth() and list_girth_goal() every refresh seconds through a DataUpdateCoordinator.
- **Show body metrics as sensors** (Home Assistant user, Home Assistant): sensor.py and sensor_configs.py create sensors for weight, BMI, body fat, water, BMR, girth values and goals, with kg or lb for weight.
- **Route calls through a proxy** (Home Assistant user, Renpho cloud API): An optional proxy setting (http:// or socks5://) is checked by check_proxy() before Renpho calls, for IPs that renpho.qnclouds.com blocks.
- **Test an account in the API** (Home Assistant user, Renpho cloud API): api/app.py is a FastAPI app with routes such as /auth, /users, /measurements and /girth_info; vercel.json deploys it and the README points to its /docs page.

### Scenario: Getting the morning weigh-in into Home Assistant

1. Copy custom_components/renpho into &lt;config_dir&gt;/custom_components/renpho/ (or install through HACS).
2. Add renpho: with email, password and refresh: 600 to configuration.yaml, plus sensor: platform: renpho.
3. Restart Home Assistant; the integration signs in to the legacy Renpho API and resolves the user id.
4. Step on the scale with the outdated Renpho app so the measurement reaches the cloud.
5. Within the next refresh cycle the weight and body-fat sensors update on the dashboard.

## Features and components

- **Coordinated refresh** — RenphoWeightCoordinator extends DataUpdateCoordinator with a configurable refresh interval. One update calls get_measurements, list_girth and list_girth_goal, then records the last-update time.
- **Errors and sensor state** — The coordinator converts timeouts and API failures into UpdateFailed. Cancellation is treated separately during shutdown. Sensor definitions and the API wrapper remain outside the polling class.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Renpho API wrapper → Cloud measurements
- Cloud measurements → Shared refreshed state

**One path through the code:** Follow _async_update_data through its three API calls and exception handling. A sensor value may be the last successful reading; the update status and timestamp are needed to distinguish it from fresh data.

## Constraints and checks

The upstream API is unofficial and the README reports breakage. This article does not establish current compatibility or medical accuracy of device measurements.

# HDR-10bpp-Display-Test: Packing ten-bit channels for a Cairo surface

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/hdr-10bpp-display-test/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/hdr-10bpp-display-test/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/HDR-10bpp-Display-Test
- Inspected revision: 9c72e072cdcae0c7d922f502049b6a155fa2daed

## Summary

This display experiment loads image data into a GTK drawing area through Cairo. Viewer3.py makes the pixel representation explicit: channel samples are masked and packed into a uint32 buffer before creating an RGB30 surface.

**Why it exists:** 10-bit HDR pipeline testing color banding and luminance curves on Linux display servers.

**Best fit:** Calibration and verification of 4K 10-bit HDR displays on Linux workstations.

## Use cases

Linux scripts to check that an HDR display really shows 10 bits per channel under an X server at depth 30.

- **Start X at depth 30** (Display tester, X server (Xorg)): Xdepth.sh runs startx -- -depth 30 and prints the depth from xwininfo, falling back to depth 24; xorg.conf sets DefaultDepth 30.
- **Show a 10-bit gray gradient** (Display tester, HDR10 monitor): Viewer.py packs the RGB channels of images/gray_gradient_10.tiff into a cairo FORMAT_RGB30 surface and draws it in a GTK 3 window.
- **Compare 8-bit and 10-bit** (Display tester, HDR10 monitor): The images/ folder holds gray_gradient_8.tiff next to gray_gradient_10.tiff, so the same gradient can be viewed at both depths to compare banding by eye.
- **Play a video at 10 bpc** (Display tester, HDR10 monitor): Viewer3.py adds a Typer CLI with --image-path and --video-path; videos are read frame by frame with imageio&#39;s ffmpeg reader in a thread at 30 fps.

### Scenario: Checking a new HDR10 monitor on Ubuntu

1. Stop the display manager: sudo systemctl stop lightdm || sudo systemctl stop gdm, then sudo pkill Xorg.
2. Start X with startx -- -depth 30 (or run Xdepth.sh).
3. Confirm with xwininfo -root | grep Depth that the root window reports depth 30.
4. Run python3 Viewer.py to open images/gray_gradient_10.tiff in the viewer window.
5. Look for banding in the gradient; smooth steps mean the 10-bit path works end to end.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 98.43 |
| Shell | 1.57 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Prerequisites

```bash
sudo apt-get install xserver-xorg python3 python3-gi python3-gi-cairo gir1.2-gtk-3.0 imagej
```

### README.md · Installing

```bash
pip3 install imageio
```

### README.md · Running the test

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/HDR-10bpp-Display-Test.git
```

### README.md · Running the test

```bash
cd HDR-10bpp-Display-Test
```

### README.md · Running the test

```bash
sudo systemctl stop lightdm || sudo systemctl stop gdm
sudo pkill Xorg
```


## Features and components

- **Pixels and drawing** — imageio reads the source array. _draw_on allocates a packed buffer and shifts each channel according to the selected depth, then passes it to cairo.ImageSurface.create_for_data. The GTK draw callback paints that surface.
- **Video path** — A worker reads video frames and updates the current image at a requested cadence. Drawing also manually processes pending GTK events. This older approach deserves particular attention to UI-thread ownership when maintained.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Image or video input → imageio array
- imageio array → Channel masking and packing
- Channel masking and packing → Cairo RGB30 surface
- Cairo RGB30 surface → GTK drawing area

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Image or video input&#34;]
  n1[&#34;imageio array&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Channel masking and packing&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Cairo RGB30 surface&#34;]
  n4[&#34;GTK drawing area&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Inspect _draw_on to see exactly where bit depth affects shifts and surface selection. Ten-bit storage concerns numeric precision; HDR transfer functions, metadata and display calibration require additional work outside this packing step.

## Constraints and checks

The lookup mentions twelve-bit input but has no matching twelve-bit Cairo format. This code does not demonstrate a complete HDR display pipeline.

# ipc-toolkit: Collision queries as a library boundary

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/ipc-toolkit/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/ipc-toolkit/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/ipc-toolkit
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 4d9e47e9f5b2afd46be99234d127d12e3c7a74cd

## Summary

ipc-toolkit provides geometric building blocks for contact-aware simulation. This fork contains collision meshes, broad-phase candidates, continuous collision detection and contact-related energies. An external simulation still owns its time stepping and solve loop.

**Why it exists:** Friction and contact physics toolkit for robust computer graphics and finite element simulation.

**Best fit:** Nonlinear continuous contact mechanics in 3D physics engines.

## Use cases

A C&#43;&#43; library with Python bindings for Incremental Potential Contact: contact barriers, CCD and friction for simulators.

- **Build a collision mesh** (Simulation developer): ipc::CollisionMesh takes vertex, edge and face matrices (Eigen), as in the README quick start.
- **Find contacts within dhat** (Simulation developer, Host simulator): NormalCollisions::build() uses a broad phase (hash grid, LBVH, sweep and prune…) to collect primitive pairs closer than dhat.
- **Evaluate barrier, derivatives** (Simulation developer, Host simulator): BarrierPotential returns the energy, gradient and sparse Hessian that the host solver adds to its objective.
- **Get a collision-free step size** (Simulation developer, Host simulator): compute_collision_free_stepsize() runs continuous collision detection (Tight Inclusion by default, nonlinear and additive variants in src/ipc/ccd) between two vertex states.
- **Add anisotropic friction** (Simulation developer, Host simulator): FrictionPotential works on TangentialCollisions; smooth_mu.hpp adds elliptical anisotropic friction coefficients (commit Anisotropic friction #210).
- **Script it from Python** (Simulation developer): pybind11 bindings under python/src expose the same API as ipctk (pip install ipctk), built when IPC_TOOLKIT_BUILD_PYTHON is ON.

### Scenario: Adding contact to one implicit time step

1. Install the bindings with pip install ipctk, or add the library to a CMake project.
2. Create a CollisionMesh from the vertices, edges and faces of the scene.
3. Build NormalCollisions with dhat = 1e-3 for the current positions.
4. Add the BarrierPotential energy, gradient and Hessian to the solver&#39;s Newton system.
5. Before accepting the Newton step, clamp it with compute_collision_free_stepsize so no surfaces cross.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| C&#43;&#43; | 94.46 |
| CMake | 2.98 |
| Python | 2.1 |
| Cuda | 0.38 |
| Dockerfile | 0.08 |

## Verified technologies

- C&#43;&#43; — Library language from repository sources
- CCD — Continuous collision detection in ipc.hpp / ipc.cpp
- CMake — CMakeLists.txt build system

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### python/README.md · Installation

```bash
pip install ipctk
```

### python/README.md · Installation

```bash
pip install git&#43;https://github.com/ipc-sim/ipc-toolkit
```

### python/README.md · Build

```bash

```

### python/README.md · Build

```bash

```

### python/README.md · CMake Build

```bash
mkdir build
cd build
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DIPC_TOOLKIT_BUILD_PYTHON=ON ..
make -j$(nproc)
```


## Features and components

- **Geometry and collision queries** — ipc.hpp accepts a CollisionMesh and vertex positions for intersection and collision-free-step queries. Broad-phase and narrow-phase CCD implementations are explicit parameters with defaults, separating candidate discovery from detailed tests.
- **Contact calculations** — The source tree separates distance, barrier, friction, tangent and potential modules. These components support a caller’s objective and derivatives; they do not automatically integrate an entire physical scene.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- External simulation → Collision mesh and vertex motion
- Collision mesh and vertex motion → Broad-phase candidates
- Broad-phase candidates → Narrow-phase CCD
- Narrow-phase CCD → Collision query result
- Collision query result → External simulation

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;External simulation&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Collision mesh and vertex motion&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Broad-phase candidates&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Narrow-phase CCD&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Collision query result&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
  n4 --&gt; n0
```

**One path through the code:** Follow is_step_collision_free from the public declaration into its implementation. Its result answers a geometric query for a proposed motion. The caller must decide how that result changes a step, line search or contact solve.

## Constraints and checks

Fork inclusion is not proof of upstream acceptance. Numerical behavior depends on caller inputs, tolerances and solver integration.

# jsonresume-theme-kendall: A JSON document into a resume template

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/jsonresume-theme-kendall/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/jsonresume-theme-kendall/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/jsonresume-theme-kendall
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: d1401cef84466c09cb84f8752c185fc96e3f5c6e

## Summary

This fork of the Kendall JSON Resume theme turns structured resume data into HTML. The renderer prepares presentation fields before handing the result to a Mustache template and the accompanying screen and print styles.

**Why it exists:** Minimalist, print-perfect resume theme supporting schema.org semantic markup and clean layout.

**Best fit:** Automated resume compilation from structured JSON data.

## Use cases

A JSON Resume theme that renders resume.json to a Bootstrap HTML page with Mustache and FontAwesome icons.

- **Render resume.json to HTML** (Resume author, resume-cli): index.js exports render(), which prepares the resume object and fills resume.template with Mustache, inlining style.css and print.css.
- **Preview the theme locally** (Resume author, resume-cli): The README runs resume serve --theme . from the theme folder and opens the preview on http://localhost:4000.
- **Show a photo or Gravatar** (Resume author, Gravatar): When basics.image is missing, render() builds a Gravatar URL from basics.email with the gravatar package.
- **Map profiles to icons** (Resume author): Each basics.profiles network is mapped to a FontAwesome class, with special cases such as stackoverflow, gitlab and keybase.
- **Print a clean copy** (Resume author): print.css is injected as a media=&#34;print&#34; style; it hides the photo and removes link URLs after anchors.

### Scenario: Previewing a resume with the Kendall theme

1. Install the CLI with npm install -g resume-cli.
2. Create and fill resume.json with resume init.
3. Run npm install in the theme folder to get mustache, lodash and gravatar.
4. Run resume serve --theme . and open http://localhost:4000.
5. Check that only filled sections (work, education, skills…) appear, then print from the browser.

- **Template and styles** — resume.template contains the HTML layout, while style.css and print.css separate screen and print appearance. The data transformation and document layout can be inspected independently.

# Kelly_RM: Kelly criterion experiments for trade sizing

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/kelly-rm/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/kelly-rm/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/AlgoETS/Kelly_RM
- Inspected revision: faf4eebf51c2b7e00b1ce6ff2fdf4400b63a9bd6


## Use cases

Notebooks and helpers to estimate trade odds from backtests and size positions with the Kelly criterion.

- **Simulate the Kelly coin game** (Quant researcher): BaseGame in Kelly_game/betting_strategies.py plays biased coin flips; Kelly, KellyWithAnEstimate, ConstantDollar and BetLikeADummy set the wager, and Playing the Game.ipynb plots wealth paths and growth rates with Altair.
- **Download price history** (Quant researcher, Market data APIs): src/data.py wraps Financial Modeling Prep historical-price-full endpoints and Binance futures klines; src/request_api.py sends the requests with httpx and src/config.py reads the API keys from the environment.
- **Optimize an RSI strategy** (Quant researcher): sandbox/Main strategy.ipynb splits each series into three training years and an unseen remainder, then grid-searches RsiOscillator bounds and window with backtesting.py and shows a seaborn heatmap.
- **Estimate win odds per ticker** (Quant researcher): From each backtest trade table the notebook computes win probability, mean and variance of win and loss sizes per ticker, on training and unseen data, and keeps tickers present in both.
- **Compute the Kelly fraction** (Quant researcher): The Kelly Criterion section applies f* = (p·b − q)/b with b = mean win size / mean loss size and stores the result in a Kelly_Fraction column.

### Scenario: Size RSI trades with the Kelly criterion

1. Run pip install -r requirements.txt, add the missing notebook packages (pandas_ta, scipy, sympy) and set FMP_API_KEY in the environment.
2. Open sandbox/Main strategy.ipynb; it reads S&amp;P 500 symbols from Wikipedia and downloads ten price histories through src/data.py.
3. Split each series into a three-year training set and an unseen set.
4. Optimize RsiOscillator with Backtest.optimize and read the parameter heatmap.
5. Compute win probability and win/loss sizes per ticker on both sets, then the Kelly fraction for each kept ticker.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Jupyter Notebook | 97.99 |
| Python | 2.01 |

# kroki-playground: An editor, an API and a renderer

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/kroki-playground/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/kroki-playground/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/kroki-playground
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 8def712a64de0f9badb65f2e1a3bb855aeb25523

## Summary

kroki-playground is a Next.js interface for editing text diagrams and previewing their output. Its server route validates the requested diagram type and format, encodes the source and fetches the rendered result from Kroki.

**Why it exists:** Serverless diagram experimentation suite in TypeScript running on Vercel with instant preview.

**Best fit:** Rapid prototyping of PlantUML, Mermaid, GraphViz, and C4 architecture diagrams.

## Use cases

A Next.js playground to write diagram source for Kroki, preview the SVG live and share it through the URL.

- **Preview a diagram live** (Diagram author, Kroki server): DiagramGenerator.tsx deflates the source with encodeDiagramPayload() (pako, base64url) and loads &lt;base&gt;/&lt;type&gt;/svg/&lt;encoded&gt; from kroki.io or NEXT_PUBLIC_KROKI_BASE_URL.
- **Switch between diagram types** (Diagram author): lib/kroki/diagramTypes.ts lists the Kroki route names (plantuml, mermaid, graphviz, d2, vega-lite…) offered in the type picker.
- **Share or download the result** (Diagram author): The page pushes ?type=…&amp;source=… into the browser history, can copy the Kroki URL to the clipboard and saves the image as diagram.svg.
- **Render through the REST API** (API client developer, Kroki server): app/api/generate-diagram/route.ts accepts GET or POST with diagramSource, selectedDiagram and outputFormat and returns base64 diagramData; the README and openapi.yaml name the path /api/generateDiagram.
- **Read the OpenAPI docs** (API client developer): /api-docs renders public/openapi.yaml with swagger-ui-react, and GET /api/openapi serves the specification.

### Scenario: Sketching a sequence diagram and sending it to a teammate

1. Run npm install then npm run dev and open http://localhost:3000.
2. Choose plantuml in the type list and paste the @startuml … @enduml source.
3. The SVG preview refreshes from Kroki as the source changes.
4. Copy the page URL, which now carries ?type=plantuml&amp;source=&lt;encoded&gt;, and send it.
5. Click download to save diagram.svg for the design document.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| TypeScript | 98.19 |
| JavaScript | 0.99 |
| CSS | 0.82 |

## Features and components

- **Validation before rendering** — app/api/generate-diagram/route.ts accepts GET and POST inputs through a shared validator. encodeDiagramPayload prepares the source for the Kroki URL. KROKI_BASE_URL selects the server-side rendering endpoint.
- **Response and failure states** — The route reads the returned bytes and responds with diagramUrl, base64 diagramData and mimeType. A non-success response from Kroki becomes a 502 with an upstream error code, distinct from invalid input.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Text editor → Next.js API route
- Next.js API route → Validate and encode
- Validate and encode → Configured Kroki service
- Configured Kroki service → Base64 result and preview
- Base64 result and preview → Text editor

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Text editor&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Next.js API route&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Validate and encode&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Configured Kroki service&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Base64 result and preview&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
  n4 --&gt; n0
```

**One path through the code:** Follow POST from req.json to validation and the upstream fetch. The response contains encoded image bytes, not raw SVG as the entire HTTP body. A consumer must use the returned MIME type when displaying those bytes.

## API



## Constraints and checks

An encoded share URL still contains recoverable diagram source. Compression and base64 encoding do not make a confidential diagram private.

# LegosTracker: LEGO catalog data and set price history

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/legostracker/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/legostracker/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/AlgoETS/LegosTracker
- Inspected revision: c24d7e7693e838f9fd3888dd566926e7dea1fd7d


## Use cases

Notebooks and a Playwright scraper to study LEGO sets with Rebrickable data and BrickEconomy price history.

- **Scrape set prices** (LEGO collector, BrickEconomy website): brickeconomy.py reads set_list.txt, opens each set on BrickEconomy with Playwright Chromium, writes &lt;set&gt;_history.csv and &lt;set&gt;_new.csv from the page charts and appends details and pricing to lego_sets.csv.
- **Explore the LEGO catalog** (LEGO collector, Rebrickable exports): general.ipynb loads the Rebrickable CSV tables in datasets/ (colors, inventories, parts, sets, themes) and plots counts such as transparent versus opaque colors.
- **Model a set&#39;s price history** (LEGO collector): analyse.ipynb cleans data/001-1_history.csv, fits linear and gradient boosting regressions on dates, projects to 2030, runs a Monte Carlo on log returns and plots the price bands in data/001-1_new.csv.
- **Compare scraped set prices** (LEGO collector): analyse.ipynb loads data/lego_sets.csv, strips currency symbols and reports the lowest and highest Quick Buy price and the average Pricing value.
- **Update collection values** (LEGO collector, BrickEconomy website): price.ipynb reads mycollection.csv, looks up each set on BrickEconomy search with requests and BeautifulSoup for retail and current values, and writes updated_mycollection.csv.

### Scenario: Track the price of set 001-1

1. Install playwright, pydantic and aiohttp and run playwright install, as in brickeconomy.ipynb.
2. List set numbers such as 001-1 in set_list.txt, one per line.
3. Run python brickeconomy.py; a visible Chromium window searches BrickEconomy and opens each set page.
4. Move the generated 001-1_history.csv, 001-1_new.csv and lego_sets.csv into data/, where analyse.ipynb reads them.
5. Run analyse.ipynb to plot the history, fit the regressions and simulate future prices.

# linkshare: A Rails application for shared links

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/linkshare/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/linkshare/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/linkshare
- Inspected revision: 2e223f99a50c07f3e60377f6c3252051b815c468

## Summary

linkshare is an archived Rails learning project for sharing links, commenting and voting. It renders pages on the server and includes account management and an administrative interface.

**Why it exists:** Ruby on Rails social site where members share links or files, vote, comment and see Embedly preview cards.

**Best fit:** Social bookmarking and rich link curation.

## Use cases

A Ruby on Rails 4.1 social site where signed-in users share links or files, vote, comment and preview pages.

- **Share a link or a file** (Member): LinksController#create saves a Link with title, url and description; the Link model also mounts a CarrierWave FileUploader, and /files/new reuses the same form.
- **Preview a shared page** (Member, Embedly): The feed and link views add embedly-card anchors, and application.js calls embedly(&#39;card&#39;, …) to render a preview card or tooltip.
- **Vote and comment on links** (Member): PUT /links/:id/like and /dislike use acts_as_votable, and nested /links/:link_id/comments routes attach comments to a link.
- **Search links and users** (Member): Link.search and User.search filter by title or name with LIKE; the feed is paginated five links per page with will_paginate, and user cards show an online indicator.
- **Manage content in /admin** (Administrator): config/routes.rb mounts RailsAdmin at /admin, and the users table has an admin flag.

### Scenario: Posting an article and collecting reactions

1. Start the app as in the README: rails server -p 8080 -b 0.0.0.0, with redis-server running.
2. Sign up at /users/sign_up with a name and the required avatar image.
3. Open /links/new, paste the article URL with a title and description, then submit.
4. On the home feed, hover the title to see the Embedly preview with vote and comment counts.
5. Other members like the link with PUT /links/:id/like and reply under /links/:id/comments.

## Features and components

- **Resources and actions** — config/routes.rb maps links to resource actions and nests comments beneath links. Member routes send like and dislike actions to upvote and downvote. The root page is links#index.
- **Accounts and administration** — Devise supplies the account-route surface, and RailsAdmin is mounted under /admin. Controllers and models are separate from the routing file; declaring a route does not show its full authorization or persistence behavior.

# LLM2SVG: Dataset analysis before model claims

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/llm2svg/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/llm2svg/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/LLM2SVG
- Inspected revision: a8337761b49bbdcbac24f58c6adc5f17d1ac2a07

## Summary

This LLM2SVG fork contains SVG dataset utilities and an evaluation-oriented scaffold. The visible implementation is useful for inspecting examples and constraints; it does not establish a completed or trained text-to-SVG model.

**Why it exists:** Structured prompt engineering framework and Python validator generating crisp, valid SVG illustrations from LLM responses.

**Best fit:** Automated vector icon and diagram generation for design systems.

## Use cases

Python utilities and data for a text-to-SVG challenge: load prompts, check SVG rules, build and render shapes.

- **Load prompts and SVG samples** (ML researcher): SVGDataLoader in utils/data_loader.py reads data/train/train.csv and data/test/test.csv and collects the SVG files stored under data/train/svg/&lt;id&gt;/; SVGDataset in utils/svg_dataset.py wraps them as a PyTorch Dataset.
- **Validate SVG constraints** (ML researcher): SVGConstraints.validate_svg in utils/svg_constraints.py rejects files over 10,000 bytes and any element or attribute outside the allowlist, parsing with defusedxml.
- **Extract terms from a prompt** (ML researcher): TextParser in utils/text_parser.py pulls colours, shapes, patterns, materials, clothing, landscape and architecture terms from a description and picks a primary category.
- **Build SVG from primitives** (ML researcher): utils/svg_utils.py has helpers for rect, circle, ellipse, path, polygon, line and group elements, a colour palette generator, generate_shapes and optimize_svg to shorten numbers.
- **Render SVG to PNG** (ML researcher, cairosvg renderer): svg_to_png in utils/svg_utils.py calls cairosvg.svg2png and either writes a file or returns PNG bytes.
- **Report on the SVG dataset** (ML researcher): SVGAnalyzer in utils/svg_analyzer.py counts SVGs, measures their sizes, tallies elements, validates every file and plots a size histogram against the 10 KB limit.

### Scenario: Check a set of candidate SVGs before submission

1. Point SVGDataLoader at the local data/ folder (the default path is hard-coded to the author’s Windows drive).
2. Read the prompts from data/train/train.csv, for example &#34;a starlit night over snow-covered peaks&#34;.
3. Run SVGAnalyzer.validate_all_svgs(&#34;train&#34;) to test every SVG under data/train/svg/ with SVGConstraints.
4. Call generate_summary_report to get a table of sizes and inferred sources, then plot_svg_size_distribution.
5. Render a passing SVG with svg_to_png to compare it with the prompt.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 100 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Dependencies

```bash
pip install cairosvg torch torchvision
```


## Features and components

- **Loading and constraints** — SVGAnalyzer composes SVGDataLoader and SVGConstraints. It enumerates samples, records file sizes and checks constraints. Dataset loading and validation are separate responsibilities.
- **Dataset reports** — The analyzer counts element names and builds per-sample validation results, with a summary-report method returning a pandas DataFrame. Element counting uses a regular expression to tolerate malformed SVG text.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- SVG dataset files → SVGDataLoader
- SVGDataLoader → Element and size analysis
- SVGDataLoader → Constraint checks
- Element and size analysis → Dataset report
- Constraint checks → Dataset report

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;SVG dataset files&#34;]
  n1[&#34;SVGDataLoader&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Element and size analysis&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Constraint checks&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Dataset report&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n1 --&gt; n3
  n2 --&gt; n4
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Follow validate_all_svgs and compare it with analyze_elements. Passing the declared constraints and having a plausible set of element names are different checks; neither establishes visual similarity to a text prompt.

## Constraints and checks

The analyzer has a machine-specific default data path. Model quality, training results and evaluation scores should not be inferred from these utility files.

# Maestro: Sheet music through an external conversion pipeline

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/maestro/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/maestro/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/Maestro
- License: AGPL-3.0
- Inspected revision: 6dca488e6e0e6bc444d3e57d6d3d62bad4ca4783

## Summary

This Maestro fork connects a React upload interface to a Spring backend and external music-conversion tools. Turning a score image into MIDI passes through an optical-recognition stage and an intermediate score representation.

**Why it exists:** Optical Music Recognition (OMR) pipeline translating sheet music scans into MIDI score sequences.

**Best fit:** Digitization of physical sheet music for playback and editing.

## Use cases

Web app that turns a scanned music sheet (PDF, PNG, JPG) into a MIDI file, with optional tempo overrides.

- **Upload a music sheet** (Musician): The React form in maestro-app/src/pages/MusicSheetUploadForm/MusicSheetUploadForm.tsx takes a dropped file and a MIDI file name, then useMaestroClient.ts checks GET /health before posting to /convert.
- **Set tempos per measure** (Musician): The form keeps a list of tempo, measure and force entries (default 120 at measure 1) and sends it as the JSON field tempos.
- **Recognize notes with Audiveris** (Audiveris OMR engine): POST /convert in ConvertController.java checks the file (10 MB limit, PDF/JPG/PNG signature) and AudiverisController.java runs Audiveris in batch mode to export a .mxl file.
- **Convert MusicXML to MIDI** (music21 (Python)): backend/src/main/MxlToMidi.py loads the .mxl with music21, applies dynamics and the requested tempo marks, and writes the .mid file.
- **Download the MIDI file** (Musician): The backend returns the .mid as an attachment and the frontend saves it with js-file-download; input and output folders are cleaned three seconds later.
- **Switch English or French** (Musician): LanguageSwitcher.tsx toggles i18next between en-US and fr-CA, using the strings in maestro-app/public/locales/.

### Scenario: Turn a PDF score into a MIDI file locally

1. Copy the Audiveris bin and lib folders into backend/audiveris/dist as backend/README.md explains.
2. Start both services with docker-compose up -d (backend on port 8080, frontend on port 3000).
3. Open localhost:3000, drop a PDF score and enter a MIDI file name.
4. Add a tempo row, for example 90 at measure 1, and submit the form.
5. The backend runs Audiveris, then MxlToMidi.py, and the browser downloads the .mid file.

| --- | ---: |

## Features and components

- **Upload boundary** — ConvertController accepts multipart uploads at /convert. It rejects empty files, checks the 10 MiB size limit and calls a file-signature validator before saving the input. Optional tempo input travels with the conversion request.
- **External processes** — AudiverisController builds an OS-dependent command and waits for the Audiveris process. The backend also includes MxlToMidi.py. Process startup, intermediate files and the returned download are separate failure points.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- React file upload → Spring validation
- Spring validation → Audiveris recognition
- Audiveris recognition → MusicXML conversion stage
- MusicXML conversion stage → MIDI download

```mermaid
flowchart LR

  n4[&#34;MIDI download&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Follow /convert into the file checks, then inspect how AudiverisController chooses its executable and output directory. A successful HTTP upload is only the start; conversion also depends on the external tool and generated files.

## Constraints and checks

Recognition accuracy depends on the score image and recognition engine. Shared output paths and shell commands deserve review before supporting concurrent public uploads.

# marketwatch: A client around a virtual trading game

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/marketwatch/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/marketwatch/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/marketwatch
- License: Apache-2.0
- Inspected revision: 9a8bd76c464501f249aff141f1e105e7345155c6

## Summary

marketwatch is an archived Python client for MarketWatch’s virtual trading game. It wraps login, game queries and simulated order operations. These are game interactions, not connections to a brokerage account.

**Why it exists:** Robust Python client library scraping and wrapping the MarketWatch virtual stock market game API.

**Best fit:** Automated trading bot development and portfolio backtesting.

## Use cases

Python client for the MarketWatch stock game: quotes, trades, portfolios and watchlists (login now blocked by captcha).

- **Get a stock price** (Game player, MarketWatch website): MarketWatch.get_price in marketwatch/__init__.py fetches the stock page with httpx and reads the intraday price with BeautifulSoup; the README marks it as working with skip_login=True.
- **Buy, sell, short or cover** (Game player, MarketWatch website): buy, sell, short and cover build an order payload and submit it to a game; MarketWatchGame in marketwatch/game.py binds the same calls to one game ID.
- **Read portfolio and orders** (Game player, MarketWatch website): get_portfolio, get_positions, get_pending_orders, get_leaderboard and get_game_settings scrape game pages; cancel_order and cancel_all_orders remove pending orders.
- **Manage watchlists** (Game player, MarketWatch website): create_watchlist, add_to_watchlist, get_watchlists, delete_watchlist and delete_watchlist_item call the MarketWatch watchlist endpoints.
- **Serve HTML game cards** (Game player, MarketWatch website): api/app.py is a FastAPI app with HTTP Basic auth that renders Jinja2 templates for /game, /portfolio, /leaderboard, /card and /watchlist.
- **Trade on an EMA crossover** (GitHub Actions, MarketWatch website): .github/workflows/ema-workflow.yml runs on a five-minute cron, pulls prices with yfinance, computes 20 and 80 period EMAs and buys or sells 100 shares on a crossover.

### Scenario: Check a quote, then trade in a game

1. Install the package with pip install marketwatch.
2. Create MarketWatch(email, password, skip_login=True) and call get_price(&#34;AAPL&#34;).
3. For game calls, log in with real credentials; the README warns this step currently fails on a captcha.
4. Once logged in, call get_games(), then buy(game_id, &#34;AAPL&#34;, 100).
5. Check the result with get_positions(game_id) and get_pending_orders(game_id).

# MarkokChainMonteCarlo: Monte Carlo and Markov chain backtests

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/markokchainmontecarlo/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/markokchainmontecarlo/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/AlgoETS/MarkokChainMonteCarlo
- Inspected revision: 96c96e249b3d51b63c348f38f4c4f37b67c0baf9


## Use cases

Notebooks that simulate AAPL prices with Monte Carlo and a Markov chain, then backtest a strategy built on them.

- **Split prices at 2023** (Quant researcher, FMP market data API): mcmc.ipynb and backtest.ipynb download the full AAPL history with get_historical_price_full_stock and split it at 2023-01-01 into prices_before_january_2023 and prices_after_january_2023.
- **Simulate Monte Carlo paths** (Quant researcher): monte_carlo_simulation draws daily shocks from the drift and volatility of log returns; mcmc.ipynb adds variants with rolling volatility and occasional extreme moves, run for 364 days with 1,000 or 10,000 paths.
- **Simulate a Markov chain** (Quant researcher): Training closes are cut into $10 bins from 0 to 200; pandas.crosstab builds the normalized transition matrix and markov_chain_simulation samples a sequence of bins.
- **Backtest MCMCStrategy** (Quant researcher): backtest.ipynb runs MCMCStrategy (5% stop loss, take profit drawn from a simulated path) and BuyAndHoldStrategy with backtesting.py: 10,000 cash, 0.2% commission, exclusive orders, on both periods.
- **Fit a linear trend** (Quant researcher): The Linear Regression section of mcmc.ipynb fits scikit-learn LinearRegression on the day index of both periods with an 80/20 train_test_split.

### Scenario: Compare MCMCStrategy with buy and hold on AAPL

1. Install the packages from the README pip command and put your own key in the FMP_API_KEY cell.
2. Open backtest.ipynb and download the AAPL history with get_historical_price_full_stock.
3. Split the data at 2023-01-01 and build the price-bin transition matrix from the earlier part.
4. Create Backtest objects for MCMCStrategy and BuyAndHoldStrategy on both periods and call run().
5. Plot the result; output/MCMCStrategy.html is a saved backtesting.py chart of MCMCStrategy.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Jupyter Notebook | 93 |
| HTML | 7 |

### README.md · Installation

```bash
pip install panda lxml bs4 httpx backtesting yfinance pandas_ta scipy rich TA-Lib
```

# MediaBoxDockerCompose: A media stack connected by volumes and networks

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/mediaboxdockercompose/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/mediaboxdockercompose/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/MediaBoxDockerCompose
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: 57d930a836819f7fd3a3421ee5ece5efe3e41778

## Summary

MediaBoxDockerCompose brings several homelab services together in Docker Compose. Service definitions, shared filesystem paths and network connections describe how they work together.

**Why it exists:** Comprehensive GitOps container stack combining WireGuard VPN tunnel networking with 15&#43; homelab automation services.

**Best fit:** Automated, isolated private cloud media server with remote access and encrypted traffic routing.

## Use cases

Docker Compose stack for a home media server: download automation, Plex/Jellyfin, admin tools and a Caddy proxy.

- **Start the media stack** (Homelab admin, Docker host): docker-compose.yml defines about twenty containers that share PUID, PGID, TZ and ROOT from .env; docker-compose up -d starts them all.
- **Automate media downloads** (Homelab admin, Docker host): Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr and Bazarr handle TV, movies, music and subtitles, fed by Jackett, Prowlarr or NZBHydra2 and sent to Deluge or NZBGet, all under ${ROOT}.
- **Watch or request media** (Media viewer, Docker host): Plex (port 32400) and Jellyfin (port 8096) serve the library; Ombi and Jellyseerr take requests and Tautulli reports Plex activity.
- **Monitor and browse the host** (Homelab admin, Docker host): Netdata (port 19999) shows host metrics, FileBrowser gives web file access and Dashmachine (port 5000) is a start page configured by dashmachine/config.ini.
- **Publish services via Caddy** (Homelab admin): caddy/Caddyfile maps subdomains such as sonarr.{$DOMAIN} to local ports with logging, rate limiting, an IP allowlist and basic auth taken from caddy/.env.
- **Add optional extras** (Homelab admin, Docker host): Separate compose files under extra/ add Samba shares, a WireGuard access server and Portainer; whisper/docker-compose.yml runs a Whisper ASR web service on port 9000.

### Scenario: Bring up a TV and movie server on one machine

1. Install Docker and Docker Compose, then clone the repository.
2. Edit .env: set TZ, PUID, PGID, ROOT (for example /media/MediaBox) and PLEX_CLAIM.
3. Run docker-compose up -d from the repository root.
4. Open Prowlarr on port 9696 and Sonarr on port 8989 to connect indexers and the download client.
5. Point Plex (port 32400) or Jellyfin (port 8096) at the completed folders under ROOT and start watching.

## Verified technologies

- Docker Compose — docker-compose.yml multi-service stack
- WireGuard VPN — Secure VPN tunnel integration
- Whisper AI — Automated audio transcription worker
- Portainer — Container management interface

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Usage

```bash
docker-compose up -d
```


### Docker

```bash
docker-compose up -d
```

## Features and components

- **Service roles** — The compose file includes download clients and media-management services such as Deluge, Jackett, Sonarr and Radarr. Each container has its own image and configuration. README service links should be distinguished from services actually enabled in Compose.
- **Persistent paths** — Volume mappings connect container paths to host storage. A path used by one service must agree with the path seen by another when files move between them. Networking and persistence solve different integration problems.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Compose service definitions → Download containers
- Compose service definitions → Media-management containers
- Download containers → Shared host storage
- Media-management containers → Shared host storage

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Compose service definitions&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Download containers&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Media-management containers&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Shared host storage&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n0 --&gt; n2
  n1 --&gt; n3
  n2 --&gt; n3
```

**One path through the code:** Choose one service and compare its mounted download and library paths with the service that consumes them. Then check its network and port settings. Two healthy containers can still disagree about where a file exists.

| Service | Runtime | Ports | Depends on |

| portainer | portainer/portainer-ce | 9443:9443 |  |
| samba | dperson/samba | 139:139, 445:445 |  |

## Constraints and checks

Image tags and external services age independently. Review credentials, published ports and host permissions before starting this personal stack elsewhere.

# MistubaVideo

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/mistubavideo/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/mistubavideo/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/ETSim/MistubaVideo
- Inspected revision: 87b180b9f03333b773fecd7708be86c75b1f822d


## Use cases

Mitsuba 3 tools from ETSim that path-trace OBJ sequences and wear-field recordings into frames, MP4 videos and GIFs.

- **Render an OBJ sequence** (Simulation researcher, Mitsuba 3 and FFmpeg): python main.py multi --folder exports --regex &#34;\d&#43;\.obj&#34; builds a scene XML per matching OBJ, renders it on CPU or CUDA at the chosen spp and resolution, then encodes MP4 and GIF with FFmpeg.
- **Render several camera views** (Simulation researcher): --view front --view top or --all-views renders each frame from the front, back, left, right, top, bottom or perspective camera defined in src/mitsuba/camera.py, with the view name in the file name.
- **Denoise and split AOVs** (Simulation researcher, Mitsuba 3 and FFmpeg): python main.py denoise &lt;path&gt; runs the OptiX denoiser from src/mitsuba/denoising.py on rendered images, and python main.py aov &lt;file.exr&gt; extracts the AOV layers of an EXR into separate files.
- **Make a field video** (Simulation researcher, Mitsuba 3 and FFmpeg): mitsuba-video render &lt;manifest.json&gt; -q paper path-traces rigid bodies at their recorded poses with a field-driven material blend and heatmap, adds a UV atlas panel and a covered-area chart, and encodes an MP4.
- **Render a wear recording** (Simulation researcher, TextureFriction runs): python main.py wear render simulation_&lt;ts&gt; or tf-render reads a TextureFriction --record folder or .h5 file through the texturefriction source.
- **Write and check a manifest** (Simulation researcher): Any project can emit a versioned manifest.json with ManifestWriter; mitsuba-video validate checks it against manifest-v1.schema.json, and mitsuba-video fixture creates a small synthetic example.

### Scenario: Render the demo field video

1. Install FFmpeg and Mitsuba 3, then run pip install -e &#34;packages/mitsuba_video[texturefriction]&#34; to get mitsuba-video and tf-render.
2. Create a synthetic input with mitsuba-video fixture demo.
3. Check the framing quickly with mitsuba-video preview demo.
4. Run mitsuba-video render demo -q preview to path-trace the frames and encode the MP4.
5. For real data, point python main.py wear render at a TextureFriction simulation_&lt;ts&gt; folder with -q paper.

| --- | ---: |

### README.md · Command-line Options

```bash
Options:
  -f, --folder TEXT               Folder containing OBJ files  [required]
  -r, --regex TEXT                Regex pattern for OBJ filenames  [default: \d&#43;\.obj]
  -n, --name TEXT                 Base name for output files  [default: multi_obj]
  -t, --threaded                  Enable multi-threading
  -w, --workers INTEGER           Max worker threads (if threaded)
  --video / --no-video            Enable video creation  [default: video]
  --gif / --no-gif                Enable GIF creation  [default: gif]
  -d, --device TEXT               Rendering device (cpu/cuda)  [default: cpu]
  -s, --spp INTEGER               Samples per pixel  [default: 256]
  --width INTEGER                 Output image width  [default: 1920]
  --height INTEGER                Output image height  [default: 1080]
```




### packages/mitsuba_video/README.md · Install and run

```bash

mitsuba-video fixture demo                                   # synthetic manifest to try things on
mitsuba-video inspect demo
mitsuba-video preview demo                                   # 960x540, 16 spp, every 8th frame
mitsuba-video render  demo -q paper --camera orbit --title &#34;Wear on a plane&#34; --ramp 0.2
mitsuba-video encode  demo/render_heatmap --fps 15 --hold 4  # new fps/title without re-rendering
mitsuba-video render  demo --resume                          # continue an interrupted render
```

# nova-backtest: Historical candles into a strategy simulation

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/nova-backtest/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/nova-backtest/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/nova-backtest
- License: MIT
- Inspected revision: dda19e6e09bdd59dd483a964f2e47085d2a1bdef

## Summary

nova-backtest is an archived fork of a strategy-backtesting framework. The core class selects an exchange client, loads a historical interval and manages a simulated bankroll and position constraints.

**Why it exists:** Financial backtesting framework interfacing with centralized crypto exchange APIs for quantitative strategy testing.

**Best fit:** Algorithmic trading strategy validation on historical tick data.

## Use cases

Python library to download crypto exchange candles and backtest a trading strategy with profit and drawdown stats.

- **Download historical candles** (Strategy developer, Exchange REST API): BackTest.get_historical_data in novalabs-backtest/utils/backtest.py calls the exchange client and caches OHLCV data in database/&lt;exchange&gt;/hist_&lt;pair&gt;_&lt;candle&gt;.csv, starting from 2019-01-01.
- **Pick an exchange client** (Strategy developer, Exchange REST API): clients() in novalabs-backtest/clients/clients.py returns a client for Binance, Bybit, OKX, Huobi, KuCoin, MEXC, Oanda or BTCEX, each following BackTestClientInterface.
- **Define entry and exit rules** (Strategy developer): A strategy subclasses BackTest and fills build_indicators, entry_strategy (entry_signal, take_profit, stop_loss, position_size) and exit_strategy (exit_signal).
- **Run the backtest** (Strategy developer): run_backtest simulates positions per pair with exchange fees, a maximum number of positions and a maximum holding time, then plots cumulative profit.
- **Save performance statistics** (Strategy developer): The run writes results/&lt;strategy&gt;_pairs_stats.csv and results/&lt;strategy&gt;_overall_stats.json with returns, drawdown and per-pair figures.
- **Build indicator features** (Strategy developer): TechnicalIndicatorsCreation in novalabs-backtest/utils/indicators.py adds lags, close ratios and support or resistance levels to a candle DataFrame.

### Scenario: Backtest a MACD strategy on Binance pairs

1. Install the dependencies listed in requirements.txt (the README&#39;s pip command spells the package novelabs-backtest).
2. Subclass BackTest with exchange=&#34;binance&#34;, candle=&#34;1h&#34;, list_pairs=[&#34;BTCUSDT&#34;, &#34;ETHUSDT&#34;], a start bankroll, leverage and max_pos.
3. Compute the MACD histogram in build_indicators and set entry_signal, take_profit and stop_loss in entry_strategy.
4. Call run_backtest(); missing pairs are downloaded into database/binance/ on first use.
5. Read the profit chart and the JSON and CSV files written under results/.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 99.74 |
| Dockerfile | 0.26 |

## Features and components

- **Inputs and clients** — BackTest receives exchange, strategy name, candle interval, pair list and start/end times. It constructs a client through the clients factory and loads the exchange fee assumptions from FEES.
- **Simulation state** — The constructor stores initial and current bankroll, leverage, maximum positions and holding duration. Geometric sizing is an explicit option. Reports depend on these assumptions as well as the strategy’s signals.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Exchange history → Client and candle data
- Client and candle data → Strategy signals
- Strategy signals → Position and bankroll simulation
- Position and bankroll simulation → Backtest outputs

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Exchange history&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Client and candle data&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Strategy signals&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Position and bankroll simulation&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Backtest outputs&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Read the BackTest constructor before interpreting a chart. Fees, leverage and position sizing affect the simulated equity path; changing one creates a different experiment even with identical candles.

## Constraints and checks

Historical simulations are not live execution or evidence of future returns. This fork is archived, and exchange API compatibility needs fresh testing.

## Files to read

- [novalabs-backtest/utils/backtest.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/nova-backtest/blob/Master/novalabs-backtest/utils/backtest.py)
- [novalabs-backtest/utils/constant.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/nova-backtest/blob/Master/novalabs-backtest/utils/constant.py)
- [README.md](https://github.com/antoinebou12/nova-backtest/blob/Master/README.md)

# novatorem: Music-provider data into an SVG widget

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/novatorem/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/novatorem/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/novatorem
- License: Unlicense
- Inspected revision: 5496fe08e19da0da1042236b2600e77b6df39f5d

## Summary

This novatorem fork builds music-status widgets from provider data. A Flask orchestrator handles rendering, while Spotify and Last.fm have separate modules. Album artwork supplies both an image and colors for the SVG.

**Why it exists:** Real-time dynamic GitHub profile README updater streaming live Spotify listening status.

**Best fit:** Live GitHub profile personalization and webhook integration.

## Use cases

Flask service that renders a Spotify or Last.fm now-playing card as an SVG for a GitHub profile README.

- **Show the now-playing card** (Profile owner, Spotify Web API): The catch-all route in api/orchestrator.py fetches the current track, extracts colours from the album art and returns an image/svg&#43;xml card; vercel.json maps /api/spotify to it.
- **Customize card colours** (Profile owner): Query parameters background_color, border_color, background_type, show_status and compact are validated in api/config.py before rendering the Jinja2 template chosen in api/templates.json.
- **Use Last.fm as a source** (Profile owner, Last.fm API): When only LAST_FM_API_KEY and LAST_FM_USERNAME are set, or Spotify auth fails, get_now_playing switches to api/lastfm.py, which can pull album art from Deezer.
- **Open the current song** (Profile owner, Spotify Web API): GET /redirect sends the visitor to the track URL, or to the upstream repository when nothing is playing.
- **Renew the refresh token** (Profile owner, Spotify Web API): scripts/spotify_local_auth.py captures the OAuth code on http://127.0.0.1:8000/callback and writes a new refresh token, optionally pushing it to Vercel with --update-vercel.
- **Preview the card locally** (Profile owner): python start.py creates .venv, installs requirements, starts Flask on port 5000 and opens /preview; docker-compose.yml runs the same app with a /health check.

### Scenario: Add a Spotify card to a GitHub profile

1. Create a Spotify app with the redirect URI http://127.0.0.1:8000/callback.
2. Copy .env.example to .env and fill SPOTIFY_CLIENT_ID and SPOTIFY_SECRET_ID.
3. Run python scripts/spotify_local_auth.py to obtain SPOTIFY_REFRESH_TOKEN.
4. Run python start.py and check the card at http://127.0.0.1:5000/preview.
5. Deploy to Vercel and embed &lt;deployment&gt;/api/spotify as an image linked to /redirect in the profile README.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| Python | 81.61 |
| Jinja | 16.06 |
| HTML | 1.64 |
| Dockerfile | 0.64 |
| Procfile | 0.04 |

## Features and components

- **Provider and presentation** — api/orchestrator.py owns the Flask application and rendering helpers. Provider modules sit alongside it. Configuration controls templates and palettes, keeping service-specific data access separate from SVG appearance.
- **Artwork processing** — ImageData fetches artwork once per object and reuses the bytes for base64 output and ColorThief palettes. load_image_with_fallback tries artwork, then a placeholder, then default colors when image processing fails.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Spotify or Last.fm → Provider data
- Provider data → Flask orchestrator
- Flask orchestrator → Artwork and palette fallback
- Artwork and palette fallback → SVG template response

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Spotify or Last.fm&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Provider data&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Flask orchestrator&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Artwork and palette fallback&#34;]
  n4[&#34;SVG template response&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Follow ImageData._fetch into get_base64 and get_palette. Reusing bytes avoids repeated image downloads within that object; it is not a persistent cross-request cache.

## Constraints and checks

The image fetch currently disables TLS verification with verify=False. That deserves correction before relying on remote artwork in a deployed instance.

## Files to read

- [api/orchestrator.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/novatorem/blob/master/api/orchestrator.py)
- [api/spotify.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/novatorem/blob/master/api/spotify.py)
- [api/lastfm.py](https://github.com/antoinebou12/novatorem/blob/master/api/lastfm.py)

# nxsand: A GPU grid for falling sand

- HTML page: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/nxsand/
- Markdown: https://antoineboucher.info/CV/blog/projects/notes/nxsand/index.md

- Repository: https://github.com/antoinebou12/nxsand
- Inspected revision: af70da331e9e74ce0d5bd0365e1447f42cfc97d0

## Summary

nxsand is a falling-sand simulation for Switch with a desktop development target. Materials live in an integer grid. Simulation passes update that grid, and a separate rendering path turns material identifiers into the displayed image.

**Why it exists:** Cellular automaton sand physics simulation engine running on libnx with touch and controller input.

**Best fit:** Interactive physics simulations on handheld console touchscreens.

## Use cases

Falling-sand sandbox for Nintendo Switch homebrew, simulated on the GPU with OpenGL ES 3.0, with desktop builds.

- **Paint materials on the grid** (Player, GPU (OpenGL ES 3.0)): Touch, Joy-Con or mouse input becomes brush strokes (source/sim/brush_stroke.cpp) written into the grid by shaders/paint.frag; the X button opens the material ring (source/ui/material_wheel.cpp).
- **Watch materials react** (Player, GPU (OpenGL ES 3.0)): A Margolus cellular automaton runs on ping-pong GL_R8UI textures in shaders/sim.frag or sim.comp, with reactions such as lava plus water giving stone in shaders/sim_common.glsl and the sim_rules_body.glsl it includes.
- **Save and load worlds** (Player): source/save/save.cpp stores up to three slots as JSON with base64 grids in sdmc:/switch/nxsand/ (./nxsand_save/ on desktop); Y or F5 quick-saves.
- **Tune performance settings** (Player, GPU (OpenGL ES 3.0)): settings.json and the Engine menu set sim resolution, substeps, active tiles, fragment or compute backend and the Battery Saver, Balanced or Quality presets.
- **Import a Powder Toy stamp** (Homebrew developer): nx::importTptStampJson in source/save/tpt_stamp_import.cpp maps The Powder Toy element IDs to NXSand materials and scales the stamp into the grid.
- **Build and test the NRO** (Homebrew developer): make builds build/NXSand.nro with devkitPro; make desktop and make test build the SDL2 desktop version and the CPU reference tests in tests/; CI does the same in .github/workflows/native-nro.yml.

### Scenario: Build NXSand and play a first world

1. Install devkitPro, then run dkp-pacman -S switch-dev switch-sdl2 switch-mesa switch-glm switch-freetype switch-harfbuzz.
2. Run make at the repository root to get build/NXSand.nro.
3. Copy it to sdmc:/switch/NXSand.nro and launch it from the Homebrew Menu.
4. Press X to pick Lava, paint with A, then switch to Water and pour it on the lava to see stone and smoke form.
5. Press Y to quick-save the world into sdmc:/switch/nxsand/.

## Languages (GitHub Linguist bytes)

| Language | % |
| --- | ---: |
| C&#43;&#43; | 80.07 |
| GLSL | 10 |
| Python | 4.44 |
| PowerShell | 3.32 |
| Makefile | 1.63 |
| Shell | 0.31 |
| Just | 0.23 |

## Getting started (repository commands, not run here)

### README.md · Reference versions (June 2026)

```bash
dkp-pacman -Q libnx switch-sdl2
dkp-pacman -Syu    # pull newer libnx / switch-sdl2 when available
```

### README.md · 2. Install Switch libraries

```bash
dkp-pacman -S switch-dev switch-sdl2 switch-mesa switch-glm switch-freetype switch-harfbuzz
```

### README.md · 3. Build the NRO

```bash

```

```bash

./build/NXSand
make test         # CPU reference tests, no GPU
```

### README.md · Desktop (optional)

```bash
pacman -S --needed mingw-w64-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-x86_64-make mingw-w64-x86_64-SDL2 mingw-w64-x86_64-freetype mingw-w64-x86_64-angleproject
```


## Features and components

- **Simulation state** — SimState holds dimensions, tick state and brush parameters. SimPipeline owns two textures and framebuffers and exposes paint, step, readback and upload operations. Ping-pong storage keeps the previous grid available while producing the next.
- **Backend and tests** — The fragment path uses GL_R8UI; the compute path uses GL_R32UI for imageStore. Active-tile tracking and fallback state are exposed in the pipeline. The Makefile separates CPU tests, GPU tests and the Switch application build.

## Architecture

Components and connections verified in the repository.

- Brush commands → Integer material grid
- Integer material grid → Simulation pass
- Simulation pass → Next grid texture
- Next grid texture → Integer material grid
- Next grid texture → Render pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  n0[&#34;Brush commands&#34;]
  n1[&#34;Integer material grid&#34;]
  n2[&#34;Simulation pass&#34;]
  n3[&#34;Next grid texture&#34;]
  n4[&#34;Render pipeline&#34;]
  n0 --&gt; n1
  n1 --&gt; n2
  n2 --&gt; n3
  n3 --&gt; n1
  n3 --&gt; n4
```

**One path through the code:** Follow paintDisk into grid modification, then step into the selected backend. readTexture identifies the current grid for rendering. Save readback must also account for OpenGL row orientation rather than copying a displayed screenshot.

## Constraints and checks

GPU feature support and performance depend on the device and backend. The desktop test target does not substitute for Switch hardware measurements.

- [source/sim/sim_state.hpp](https://github.com/antoinebou12/nxsand/blob/main/source/sim/sim_state.hpp)
- [Makefile](https://github.com/antoinebou12/nxsand/blob/main/Makefile)
